options.B: Because their impaired immune system cannot mount a robust inflammatory response
options.C: Because normal flora completely neutralize all pathogens
options.D: Because their skin barriers become exceptionally thick

explanation: Immunocompromised patients lack the necessary white blood cells and chemical mediators to mount a strong inflammatory and purulent response. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T2#GNS123_U4_T2_h7)

question: Which laboratory parameter is most critical for a nurse to monitor when evaluating infection risk in a patient receiving chemotherapy?

options.A: Absolute neutrophil count (ANC)
options.B: Serum sodium levels
options.C: Total red blood cell count
options.D: Prothrombin time (PT)

explanation: Monitoring the absolute neutrophil count (ANC) is vital because neutrophils are frontline phagocytes essential for fighting bacterial and fungal infections. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T2#GNS123_U4_T2_h7)

question: What is the single most effective method to prevent cross-contamination and healthcare-associated infections?

options.A: Administering prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics
options.B: Strict and meticulous hand hygiene
options.C: Restricting all visitors from the hospital ward
options.D: Prohibiting patients from eating fresh cooked food

explanation: Meticulous hand hygiene by healthcare workers is universally recognized as the most effective measure to prevent the spread of infections. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T2#GNS123_U4_T2_h8)

question: Why are live attenuated vaccines contraindicated in severely immunocompromised patients?

options.A: They cause severe allergic skin reactions immediately.
options.B: They can cause the actual disease because the patient's immune system cannot control the weakened pathogen.
options.C: They permanently destroy all existing memory T-cells.
options.D: They neutralize the effectiveness of hand hygiene products.

explanation: Live vaccines contain live, weakened pathogens that can multiply and cause active, severe infections in individuals with compromised immune systems. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T2#GNS123_U4_T2_h8)

question: What primary event defines the initiation of an infection in the human body?

options.A: Immediate antibody destruction
options.B: Pathogen invasion, multiplication, and tissue reaction
options.C: Complete sterilization of skin flora
options.D: Nutrient depletion in the gastrointestinal tract

explanation: An infection officially begins when a pathogen invades body tissues, multiplies, and triggers a local or systemic reaction. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h1)

question: Why is understanding the infection process vital for student nurses in Nigeria?

options.A: To eliminate the need for hand hygiene
options.B: To implement effective preventive strategies and break transmission cycles
options.C: To diagnose all infectious diseases without laboratory testing
options.D: To replace physicians in prescribing broad-spectrum antibiotics

explanation: Recognizing the dynamics of infection allows nurses to implement effective preventive strategies, breaking the cycle of disease transmission in healthcare and community settings. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h1)

question: Which of the following represents the correct sequence of the six links in the chain of infection?

options.A: Host, Reservoir, Portal of Entry, Pathogen, Exit, Transmission
options.B: Infectious Agent, Reservoir, Portal of Exit, Mode of Transmission, Portal of Entry, Susceptible Host
options.C: Vector, Pathogen, Transmission, Host, Reservoir, Exit
options.D: Reservoir, Susceptible Host, Agent, Entry, Exit, Transmission

explanation: The chain consists of the infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, and susceptible host in continuous sequence. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h2)

question: What is the primary significance of identifying the chain of infection in nursing practice?

options.A: It allows nurses to break any single link to stop the infection process.
options.B: It proves that all infections originate from animal reservoirs.
options.C: It determines the exact financial cost of hospital stays.
options.D: It eliminates the need for patient vital sign monitoring.

explanation: Breaking any single link in the chain stops the infection process, forming the basis of all infection control precautions. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h2)

question: Why are viruses classified as obligate intracellular parasites?

options.A: They can survive independently on dry surfaces indefinitely.
options.B: They require a living host cell to replicate.
options.C: They are easily treated with standard antibacterial soaps.
options.D: They contain complex peptidoglycan cell walls.

explanation: Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites because they must invade living host cells to reproduce and multiply. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h3)

question: Which microorganism type is primarily responsible for causing malaria in endemic regions like Nigeria?

options.A: Bacteria
options.B: Viruses
options.C: Fungi
options.D: Parasites (Plasmodium species)

explanation: Plasmodium species, which cause malaria, belong to the category of parasites that live inside a host organism. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h3)

question: Which stage of clinical infection is characterized by vague, non-specific symptoms and high contagiousness?

options.A: Incubation period
options.B: Prodromal stage
options.C: Illness stage
options.D: Convalescence stage

explanation: The prodromal stage features non-specific symptoms like fatigue and malaise, and patients are often highly contagious because they feel relatively normal. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h4)

question: What defines the incubation period of an infection?

options.A: The time between pathogen entry and the appearance of the first symptoms
options.B: The period when specific disease signs are most severe
options.C: The phase of complete recovery and tissue repair
options.D: The time when non-specific fatigue first appears

explanation: The incubation period is the exact interval between when the pathogen invades the host and when the first signs and symptoms manifest. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h4)

question: Which component of the immune system is primarily responsible for humoral immunity by producing antibodies?

options.A: T lymphocytes
options.B: B lymphocytes
options.C: Erythrocytes
options.D: Platelets

explanation: B cells are responsible for humoral immunity through the production of specific antibodies against circulating antigens. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h5)

question: What is the primary function of the inflammatory response as a nonspecific defense mechanism?

options.A: To synthesize permanent antibodies against viral strains
options.B: To deliver fluid, blood products, and nutrients to neutralize pathogens and promote healing
options.C: To permanently lower the body temperature to prevent microbial replication
options.D: To halt all blood circulation near the site of injury

explanation: Inflammation is a vascular and cellular reaction that brings protective elements to injured tissues to neutralize pathogens and facilitate tissue repair. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h5)

question: Which blood test result is commonly associated with an active bacterial infection during a Complete Blood Count (CBC)?

options.A: Leukopenia
options.B: Leukocytosis
options.C: Thrombocytopenia
options.D: Polycythemia

explanation: Bacterial infections typically trigger leukocytosis, which is an elevated white blood cell count as the body fights off the pathogen. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h6)

question: What is the primary clinical purpose of performing microbiological culture and sensitivity testing?

options.A: To measure the patient's red blood cell volume
options.B: To identify the specific causative pathogen and effective antimicrobial medications
options.C: To assess the patient's long-term nutritional status
options.D: To determine the exact stage of the incubation period

explanation: Culture and sensitivity tests identify the exact microorganism causing the infection and determine which antibiotics will successfully treat it. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h6)

question: What is considered the single most effective nursing measure for preventing healthcare-associated infections?

options.A: Wearing sterile gowns during all patient interactions
options.B: Performing proper hand hygiene before and after patient contact
options.C: Administering prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics daily
options.D: Isolating every admitted patient in a negative-pressure room

explanation: Hand hygiene is universally recognized as the single most effective intervention to stop the transmission of infectious agents in healthcare settings. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h7)

question: Why is patient education on completing a full course of prescribed antibiotics critically important?

options.A: To reduce the financial cost of hospital readmissions
options.B: To prevent the development of antimicrobial resistance
options.C: To ensure immediate normalization of white blood cell counts
options.D: To eliminate the need for standard hand hygiene practices

explanation: Completing the full course of antibiotics ensures all pathogens are eradicated, preventing surviving bacteria from developing antimicrobial resistance. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h7)

question: What serious condition occurs when pathogens enter the bloodstream and trigger a severe, life-threatening systemic inflammatory response?

options.A: Cellulitis
options.B: Sepsis
options.C: Leukocytosis
options.D: Convalescence

explanation: Sepsis occurs when bloodstream infections trigger a massive systemic inflammatory response that can lead to organ failure and shock. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h8)

question: Which of the following is a potential long-term complication of untreated or recurrent streptococcal infections?

options.A: Rheumatic heart disease
options.B: Acute localized abscess
options.C: Rapid viral immunity
options.D: Elevated platelet counts

explanation: Untreated streptococcal infections, such as strep throat, can lead to serious long-term complications like rheumatic heart disease. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T3#GNS123_U4_T3_h8)

question: What is another commonly used term for nosocomial infections?

options.A: Community-acquired infections
options.B: Healthcare-associated infections
options.C: Idiopathic clinical infections
options.D: Endogenous baseline infections

explanation: Nosocomial infections are officially referred to as healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) because they are acquired while receiving treatment in a healthcare facility. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T4#GNS123_U4_T4_h1)

question: Why are hospitalized patients particularly susceptible to nosocomial infections?

options.A: They consume a high-fiber hospital diet
options.B: They are frequently immunocompromised and undergo invasive procedures
options.C: They spend too much time outdoors walking around hospital grounds
options.D: They lack access to modern electronic devices

explanation: Hospitalized patients are often immunocompromised and subjected to invasive procedures, making them much more vulnerable to acquiring infections. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T4#GNS123_U4_T4_h1)

question: How many total links make up the standard chain of infection model?

options.A: Four
options.B: Five
options.C: Six
options.D: Seven

explanation: The chain of infection consists of six distinct links: infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, and susceptible host. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T4#GNS123_U4_T4_h2)

question: Which link in the chain of infection is directly interrupted when a nurse performs proper hand hygiene?

options.A: Infectious agent
options.B: Mode of transmission
options.C: Susceptible host
options.D: Reservoir

explanation: Hand hygiene removes pathogens from the hands, thereby breaking the mode of transmission between patients and surfaces. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T4#GNS123_U4_T4_h2)

question: To which group of patients should standard precautions be applied?

options.A: Only patients with confirmed tuberculosis
options.B: Only patients with visible blood on their skin
options.C: All patients regardless of their diagnosis or infection status
options.D: Only patients admitted to surgical wards

explanation: Standard precautions must be applied universally to all patients in the healthcare setting, regardless of their diagnosis or presumed infection status. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T4#GNS123_U4_T4_h3)

question: Which bodily excretion is specifically excluded from standard precautions fluids?

options.A: Sweat
options.B: Urine
options.C: Saliva
options.D: Sputum

explanation: Standard precautions apply to all body fluids except sweat, regardless of whether it contains visible blood. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T4#GNS123_U4_T4_h3)

question: Which type of precaution requires the use of an Airborne Infection Isolation Room (AIIR) with negative pressure?

options.A: Standard precautions
options.B: Contact precautions
options.C: Droplet precautions
options.D: Airborne precautions

explanation: Airborne precautions require negative pressure rooms to prevent infectious particles from escaping into the surrounding corridor and facility air. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T4#GNS123_U4_T4_h4)

question: What personal protective equipment is specifically emphasized for healthcare workers providing care under droplet precautions?

options.A: N95 respirator mask
options.B: Surgical mask
options.C: Sterile full-body hazmat suit
options.D: Double rubber aprons

explanation: Droplet precautions require wearing a standard surgical mask when working within close proximity to the patient to block large respiratory droplets. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T4#GNS123_U4_T4_h4)

question: According to the WHO, what is the minimum duration for performing hand washing with soap and water?

options.A: 10 to 15 seconds
options.B: 20 to 30 seconds
options.C: 40 to 60 seconds
options.D: 90 to 120 seconds

explanation: Hand washing with soap and water must last at least 40 to 60 seconds to ensure adequate removal of microorganisms from all skin surfaces. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T4#GNS123_U4_T4_h5)

question: When is it mandatory to use soap and water instead of an alcohol-based hand rub?

options.A: Before taking a patient's vital signs
options.B: When hands are visibly soiled with blood or body fluids
options.C: Immediately before entering the hospital ward
options.D: After charting on an electronic medical record

explanation: Soap and water must be used when hands are visibly dirty or soiled with blood and body fluids, as alcohol rubs do not clean physical debris. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T4#GNS123_U4_T4_h5)

question: What is the correct first step when removing (doffing) personal protective equipment?

options.A: Remove the mask
options.B: Remove the gloves
options.C: Take off the gown
options.D: Remove eye protection

explanation: Gloves are typically the most contaminated item of PPE and must be removed first during the doffing process. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T4#GNS123_U4_T4_h6)

question: Which of the following statements about medical gloves is correct?

options.A: Gloves can be washed with soap and water and reused for multiple patients
options.B: Gloves replace the need for hand hygiene after patient care
options.C: Gloves must be changed between patients and disposed of properly
options.D: Gloves are only required during surgical operations

explanation: Gloves must be changed between different patients and discarded appropriately to prevent cross-contamination, and they never replace hand hygiene. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T4#GNS123_U4_T4_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of maintaining aseptic technique during invasive procedures?

options.A: To speed up the healing time of surgical incisions
options.B: To keep objects and areas as free from microorganisms as possible
options.C: To eliminate the need for administering systemic antibiotics
options.D: To reduce the financial cost of hospital supplies

explanation: Aseptic technique is specifically designed to keep items and sterile fields as free from microorganisms as possible to prevent infection. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T4#GNS123_U4_T4_h7)

question: How should an indwelling urinary catheter collection bag be positioned to prevent CAUTIs?

options.A: Above the level of the patient's bladder
options.B: Directly on the patient's bed sheets
options.C: Below the level of the bladder at all times
options.D: Hanging from the IV pole at head height

explanation: The catheter bag must always remain below the level of the bladder to prevent urine from flowing backward into the bladder and causing an infection. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T4#GNS123_U4_T4_h7)

question: Where must used needles and scalpel blades be disposed of immediately after use?

options.A: Black domestic waste bins
options.B: Puncture-resistant safety boxes
options.C: Open cardboard boxes
options.D: Unmarked plastic shopping bags

explanation: Sharps must always be discarded directly into puncture-resistant safety boxes to prevent needlestick injuries and accidental exposure. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T4#GNS123_U4_T4_h8)

question: What is the primary function of disinfecting high-touch hospital surfaces?

options.A: To remove dust and improve room appearance
options.B: To eliminate persistent reservoirs of pathogenic microorganisms
options.C: To keep the room smelling fresh for incoming patients
options.D: To reduce the humidity levels inside the clinical ward

explanation: Regular disinfection of high-touch surfaces eliminates microbial reservoirs that could otherwise transmit infections to patients and staff. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T4#GNS123_U4_T4_h8)

question: Why are bedside nurses ideally positioned to conduct infection surveillance?

options.A: They have advanced degrees in hospital administration
options.B: They spend the most continuous time at the patient's bedside
options.C: They are solely responsible for purchasing hospital disinfectants
options.D: They work exclusively in hospital microbiology laboratories

explanation: Bedside nurses spend the most continuous time observing patients, making them uniquely qualified to detect early signs of infection and unusual clinical trends. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T4#GNS123_U4_T4_h9)

question: What action should a nurse take immediately after experiencing an occupational needlestick injury?

options.A: Hide the incident so colleagues do not worry
options.B: Report the exposure promptly to ensure proper post-exposure management
options.C: Wait until the end of the month to mention it during evaluation
options.D: Take a self-prescribed dose of broad-spectrum antibiotics

explanation: Prompt reporting of occupational exposures ensures that the healthcare worker receives immediate post-exposure prophylaxis and appropriate medical follow-up. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T4#GNS123_U4_T4_h9)

question: What distinguishes an emerging infectious disease from a re-emerging one?

options.A: Emerging diseases are always bacterial, while re-emerging are viral.
options.B: Emerging diseases have increased in incidence recently or are novel, whereas re-emerging diseases are established conditions experiencing a resurgence.
options.C: Re-emerging diseases only affect animals, while emerging diseases strictly affect humans.
options.D: Emerging diseases are untreatable, whereas re-emerging diseases respond to basic antibiotics.

explanation: Emerging infectious diseases are novel or recently increased in incidence, while re-emerging infectious diseases are established illnesses that were previously controlled but are now returning or expanding. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h1)

question: Which of the following is cited as a major contributor to the spread of emerging and re-emerging infections in Nigeria?

options.A: Stagnant population growth
options.B: Decreased international travel
options.C: Rapid population growth and unplanned urbanization
options.D: Absence of any environmental changes

explanation: Rapid population growth and unplanned urbanization create conditions that foster the spread and emergence of infectious pathogens. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h1)

question: What is a zoonotic spillover event?

options.A: The transmission of a pathogen from humans back to animal populations
options.B: The spread of a pathogen from animals to humans
options.C: The mutation of bacteria in contaminated water sources
options.D: The airborne transmission of a virus between human hosts

explanation: A zoonotic spillover event occurs when a pathogen successfully jumps and transmits from an animal reservoir to a human host. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h2)

question: How do environmental changes like deforestation impact infectious disease rates?

options.A: They completely eradicate disease vectors.
options.B: They bring animal reservoirs and insect vectors into closer contact with humans.
options.C: They purify water sources, reducing waterborne infections.
options.D: They decrease air temperature, preventing viral replication.

explanation: Deforestation and ecological shifts alter vector and animal habitats, increasing human-animal interactions and the risk of disease transmission. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h2)

question: Which animal reservoir is primarily responsible for transmitting Lassa virus to humans?

options.A: Domestic dogs
options.B: Mastomys rats
options.C: Pigs
options.D: Fruit bats

explanation: Lassa fever is primarily transmitted to humans through contact with food or items contaminated with the urine or feces of infected Mastomys rats. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h3)

question: The northern region of Nigeria is particularly susceptible to outbreaks of which disease during the dry season?

options.A: Cholera
options.B: Cerebrospinal meningitis
options.C: Yellow fever
options.D: Dengue fever

explanation: Cerebrospinal meningitis frequently peaks in northern Nigeria's meningitis belt during the dry season due to environmental factors and crowded living conditions. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h3)

question: What is the primary pathophysiological effect of viral hemorrhagic fevers on the host's vascular system?

options.A: Vasoconstriction and hypertension
options.B: Increased vascular permeability leading to shock and organ dysfunction
options.C: Thickening of the blood vessel walls preventing oxygen exchange
options.D: Complete cessation of blood flow to the extremities

explanation: Viral hemorrhagic fevers target endothelial cells, causing increased vascular permeability which can lead to severe shock and multi-organ failure. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h4)

question: Which transmission mode is most commonly associated with waterborne outbreaks of cholera?

options.A: Airborne droplets
options.B: Fecal-oral route
options.C: Vector-borne mosquito bites
options.D: Direct skin-to-skin contact

explanation: Cholera spreads primarily through the fecal-oral route, usually via contaminated water and food sources. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h4)

question: Which clinical signs are specifically indicative of meningeal irritation during a physical assessment?

options.A: Rice-water stools and skin turgor loss
options.B: Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs
options.C: Petechiae and mucosal bleeding
options.D: Jaundice and dark urine

explanation: Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs are classic physical assessment findings that indicate irritation of the meninges, commonly seen in meningitis. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h5)

question: Why is taking a detailed travel and occupational history crucial when assessing a patient with a suspected emerging infection?

options.C: It helps determine the exact room number the patient should be admitted to.
options.D: It reveals potential exposures to specific vectors, animal reservoirs, or outbreak zones.
options.A: It is required primarily for hospital billing purposes.
options.B: It replaces the need for laboratory diagnostic tests.

explanation: A thorough history uncovers clues regarding exposure risks, such as travel to outbreak areas or contact with animal vectors, which aids rapid diagnosis. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h5)

question: What is the primary function of a Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) test in diagnosing infectious diseases?

options.A: To measure the patient's exact blood pressure and heart rate
options.B: To detect specific viral or bacterial genetic material with high sensitivity
options.C: To assess kidney function through electrolyte balance
options.D: To visualize physical structural damage to organs

explanation: PCR assays are laboratory tests designed to detect the genetic material (DNA or RNA) of pathogens, offering high sensitivity and specificity. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h6)

question: What safety practice must a nurse prioritize when collecting and handling specimens from a patient with a suspected dangerous emerging pathogen?

options.A: Transporting specimens in open, unsealed containers for quick access
options.B: Strictly adhering to universal precautions, biosafety guidelines, and clear labeling
options.C: Performing the laboratory analysis directly at the patient's bedside without gloves
options.D: Discarding all laboratory request forms before specimen delivery

explanation: Strict adherence to universal precautions, biosafety rules, and proper labeling protects healthcare workers and laboratory personnel from accidental exposure. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h6)

question: What is considered the single most effective intervention for breaking the chain of infection in healthcare settings?

options.A: Administering prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics
options.B: Proper hand hygiene using soap and water or alcohol rubs
options.C: Wearing double shoe covers at all times
options.D: Restricting all patient visitors permanently

explanation: Hand hygiene is universally recognized as the single most effective measure to prevent the transmission of healthcare-associated infections. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h7)

question: When should transmission-based precautions be initiated for a patient suspected of having a highly contagious emerging infection?

options.A: Only after laboratory confirmation is fully completed
options.B: Immediately upon identification of suspicion during triage or assessment
options.C: After the patient begins showing signs of clinical recovery
options.D: Only when visitors complain about infection risks

explanation: Precautions must be initiated immediately upon suspicion or presentation of symptoms to prevent potential spread before lab confirmation is finalized. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h7)

question: Which specific antiviral medication is commonly utilized in the management of Lassa fever?

options.A: Ribavirin
options.B: Penicillin
options.C: Chloroquine
options.D: Acyclovir

explanation: Ribavirin is the specific antiviral medication used in the treatment protocols for Lassa fever, especially when administered early in the disease course. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h8)

question: What is the primary clinical goal of aggressive fluid resuscitation in conditions like cholera or severe viral infections?

options.A: To lower the patient's body temperature instantly
options.B: To combat hypovolemic shock and restore physiological stability
options.C: To dilute the concentration of white blood cells
options.D: To eliminate the need for any antibiotic therapy

explanation: Aggressive fluid resuscitation replaces lost intravascular and extracellular volume, preventing or treating hypovolemic shock and organ failure. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h8)

question: What is the primary purpose of public health surveillance systems like the IDSR in Nigeria?

options.A: To audit individual hospital financial expenditures
options.B: To systematically collect, analyze, and interpret health data for outbreak detection and response
options.C: To evaluate nursing school curricula and licensing exams
options.D: To regulate the commercial pricing of pharmaceutical drugs

explanation: Public health surveillance involves the continuous tracking and analysis of health data to detect, monitor, and respond to disease outbreaks effectively. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h9)

question: How do frontline clinical nurses directly contribute to national public health surveillance?

options.A: By manufacturing vaccines in hospital laboratories
options.B: By identifying index cases, documenting data, and reporting notifiable diseases to authorities
options.C: By drafting international health treaties and trade policies
options.D: By funding government health sector budgets

explanation: Nurses contribute by recognizing unusual cases, recording necessary data, and promptly reporting notifiable diseases to public health agencies. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h9)

question: Which specific cellular receptor does the SARS-CoV-2 virus primarily bind to via its spike glycoproteins?

options.A: Beta-2 adrenergic receptors
options.B: Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptors
options.C: Insulin receptors
options.D: Cholinergic receptors

explanation: SARS-CoV-2 uses its spike glycoproteins to bind to ACE2 receptors, which are densely populated on respiratory epithelial cells and other tissues. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T6#GNS123_U4_T6_h1)

question: What is the primary driver of severe multi-organ damage and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) in COVID-19 patients?

options.A: Bacterial coinfection in the gut
options.B: Excessive production of insulin
options.C: A dysregulated cytokine storm causing widespread inflammation
options.D: Rapid depletion of red blood cells

explanation: A severe cytokine storm leads to a hyperinflammatory response, resulting in endothelial injury, microvascular thrombosis, and multi-organ failure. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T6#GNS123_U4_T6_h1)

question: What is the primary mode of transmission for the SARS-CoV-2 virus?

options.A: Vector-borne transmission via mosquitoes
options.B: Respiratory droplets and aerosols
options.C: Fecal-oral route through contaminated food
options.D: Direct contact with intact skin

explanation: SARS-CoV-2 spreads primarily when an infected person expels respiratory droplets and aerosols through breathing, talking, coughing, or sneezing. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T6#GNS123_U4_T6_h2)

question: Which level of personal protective equipment (PPE) is mandatory for healthcare workers performing aerosol-generating procedures (AGPs) on COVID-19 patients?

options.A: Simple cloth mask and gloves
options.B: N95 or FFP2 respirator with eye protection, gown, and gloves
options.C: Surgical mask only
options.D: Heavy-duty rubber apron and boots

explanation: Airborne precautions during AGPs require an N95 or equivalent respirator, eye protection, gown, and gloves to protect against high-risk aerosol exposure. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T6#GNS123_U4_T6_h2)

question: What oxygen saturation (SpO2) threshold on room air helps distinguish moderate COVID-19 from severe COVID-19 disease?

options.A: Less than 93%
options.B: Exactly 95%
options.C: Greater than 98%
options.D: Between 99% and 100%

explanation: An SpO2 of less than 93% on room air is a key clinical indicator of severe COVID-19 requiring supplemental oxygen therapy. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T6#GNS123_U4_T6_h3)

question: Which of the following defines critical COVID-19 illness?

options.A: Mild upper respiratory symptoms and normal chest X-ray
options.B: Fever and fatigue without any respiratory distress
options.C: Presence of ARDS, septic shock, or multi-organ failure
options.D: Loss of taste and smell without fever

explanation: Critical illness involves life-threatening complications such as ARDS, septic shock, and multi-organ dysfunction requiring ICU-level care. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T6#GNS123_U4_T6_h3)

question: What is considered the gold standard diagnostic test for detecting active SARS-CoV-2 infection?

options.A: Complete Blood Count (CBC)
options.B: Reverse Transcription-Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR)
options.C: Chest X-ray
options.D: Rapid antibody blood test

explanation: RT-PCR testing on respiratory specimens is the gold standard due to its high sensitivity and specificity in detecting viral RNA. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T6#GNS123_U4_T6_h4)

question: Which laboratory finding is commonly associated with a hypercoagulable state and increased thrombosis risk in severe COVID-19 patients?

options.A: Elevated D-dimer
options.B: High platelet count
options.C: Low serum creatinine
options.D: Elevated white blood cell count

explanation: Elevated D-dimer levels indicate ongoing fibrin degradation and reflect the heightened risk of blood clots in severe COVID-19 cases. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T6#GNS123_U4_T6_h4)

question: What is 'happy hypoxemia' in the context of COVID-19 nursing assessment?

options.A: A patient who is extremely anxious and hyperventilating
options.B: A patient with dangerously low oxygen saturation who reports no severe shortness of breath
options.C: A patient whose fever resolves spontaneously
options.D: A patient who experiences euphoria from oxygen therapy

explanation: Happy hypoxemia refers to patients who have critically low blood oxygen levels without displaying typical distress or shortness of breath. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T6#GNS123_U4_T6_h5)

question: Why is precise fluid balance charting important when monitoring hospitalized COVID-19 patients?

options.A: To calculate the exact caloric intake required
options.B: To prevent both fluid overload and dehydration
options.C: To determine the need for immediate blood transfusions
options.D: To monitor liver enzyme production

explanation: Strict monitoring of intake and output prevents fluid overload (which can worsen pulmonary edema) and dehydration. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T6#GNS123_U4_T6_h5)

question: Which pharmacological agent is routinely administered to hospitalized COVID-19 patients requiring supplemental oxygen to reduce mortality by dampening inflammation?

options.A: Dexamethasone
options.B: Aspirin
options.C: Amoxicillin
options.D: Ibuprofen

explanation: Dexamethasone is a corticosteroid proven to decrease mortality in patients needing oxygen by reducing harmful systemic inflammation. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T6#GNS123_U4_T6_h6)

question: Why is low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) commonly prescribed for hospitalized COVID-19 patients?

options.A: To lower elevated blood glucose levels
options.B: To prevent venous thromboembolism and blood clots
options.C: To stimulate red blood cell production
options.D: To act as a direct antiviral agent

explanation: COVID-19 creates a hypercoagulable state, making thromboprophylaxis with LMWH essential to prevent dangerous blood clots. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T6#GNS123_U4_T6_h6)

question: What is a primary clinical benefit of High-Flow Nasal Cannula (HFNC) therapy in COVID-19 management?

options.A: It completely replaces the need for nursing monitoring.
options.B: It delivers heated and humidified oxygen at high rates, often reducing the need for invasive intubation.
options.C: It acts as a broad-spectrum antibiotic.
options.D: It permanently cures the underlying viral infection.

explanation: HFNC provides high-flow, conditioned oxygen that supports breathing and can prevent the need for mechanical ventilation in moderate-to-severe cases. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T6#GNS123_U4_T6_h7)

question: For how many hours a day is prone positioning typically recommended for mechanically ventilated COVID-19 patients with refractory hypoxemia?

options.A: 1 to 2 hours
options.B: 4 to 6 hours
options.C: 12 to 16 hours
options.D: 24 continuous hours

explanation: Proning patients for 12 to 16 hours daily improves ventilation-perfusion matching and oxygenation in acute respiratory distress. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T6#GNS123_U4_T6_h7)

question: What term describes the condition where patients experience persistent symptoms weeks or months after recovering from acute COVID-19?

options.A: Acute respiratory distress syndrome
options.B: Long COVID or post-COVID-19 condition
options.C: Cytokine storm syndrome
options.D: Transient ischemic attack

explanation: Long COVID refers to ongoing physical and cognitive symptoms that linger long after the initial acute phase of the infection has passed. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T6#GNS123_U4_T6_h8)

question: Which of the following is a common manifestation of Long COVID affecting cognitive function?

options.A: Acute renal failure
options.B: Brain fog and difficulty concentrating
options.C: Uncontrolled hypertension
options.D: Spontaneous bone fractures

explanation: Cognitive symptoms such as 'brain fog,' memory issues, and difficulty concentrating are frequently reported by individuals with long COVID. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T6#GNS123_U4_T6_h8)

question: What is considered the most effective public health measure for preventing severe illness, hospitalization, and death from COVID-19?

options.A: Regular use of herbal steam inhalations
options.B: Widespread vaccination and booster doses
options.C: Complete isolation of entire cities indefinitely
options.D: Taking prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics daily

explanation: Vaccination is scientifically proven to be the most effective intervention for preventing severe COVID-19 disease and reducing mortality. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T6#GNS123_U4_T6_h9)

question: What is an essential educational responsibility for nurses when communicating with community members about COVID-19 prevention?

options.A: Discouraging hand hygiene to build natural tolerance
options.B: Debunking health misinformation and explaining correct mask usage
options.C: Instructing patients to ignore mild symptoms completely
options.D: Advocating against the use of any protective guidelines

explanation: Nurses play a key role in providing accurate information, promoting correct preventive habits like mask usage, and dispelling dangerous myths. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T6#GNS123_U4_T6_h9)

question: What is the primary purpose of the nursing process in clinical practice?

options.A: To replace the need for physician orders
options.B: To provide a systematic framework for delivering individualized patient care
options.C: To document hospital financial expenditures
options.D: To replace the need for interprofessional communication

explanation: The nursing process is a systematic, problem-solving framework designed to guide nurses in delivering organized, patient-centered care. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T7#GNS123_U4_T7_h1)

question: Which of the following correctly lists the five phases of the nursing process in order?

options.A: Diagnosis, Assessment, Planning, Evaluation, Implementation
options.B: Assessment, Nursing Diagnosis, Planning, Implementation, Evaluation
options.C: Planning, Implementation, Assessment, Evaluation, Diagnosis
options.D: Evaluation, Assessment, Implementation, Diagnosis, Planning

explanation: The five standard phases flow logically from gathering data to diagnosing, planning, executing, and finally assessing the outcomes. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T7#GNS123_U4_T7_h1)

question: Which of the following represents an example of subjective data?

options.A: Blood pressure of 130/80 mmHg
options.B: Patient report of severe lower back pain
options.C: A surgical wound showing mild redness
options.D: Serum potassium level of 4.2 mEq/L

explanation: Subjective data consists of symptoms or information reported directly by the patient that cannot be independently measured by the nurse. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T7#GNS123_U4_T7_h2)

question: Why is data validation a crucial step during the assessment phase?

options.A: It ensures that nursing diagnoses are based on accurate and reliable information
options.B: It replaces the need to document physical examination findings
options.C: It allows the nurse to prescribe medications independently
options.D: It eliminates the need for secondary data sources

explanation: Validating data ensures that the information gathered is accurate and complete, preventing errors in subsequent clinical judgments. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T7#GNS123_U4_T7_h2)

question: How does a nursing diagnosis differ primarily from a medical diagnosis?

options.A: A medical diagnosis focuses on human responses, whereas a nursing diagnosis identifies disease pathology.
options.B: A nursing diagnosis identifies human responses to health conditions and can change, whereas a medical diagnosis identifies the disease.
options.C: A nursing diagnosis is made exclusively by physicians.
options.D: A medical diagnosis is based on NANDA-I terminology.

explanation: Medical diagnoses name the underlying disease process, while nursing diagnoses describe the patient's physical and emotional response to health issues. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T7#GNS123_U4_T7_h3)

question: What do the letters in the traditional PES format for a problem-focused nursing diagnosis stand for?

options.A: Patient, Evaluation, Symptoms
options.B: Plan, Etiology, Solution
options.C: Problem, Etiology, Signs and symptoms
options.D: Priority, Evidence, Standard

explanation: PES stands for Problem (the NANDA label), Etiology (related factors), and Signs and symptoms (defining characteristics). [learn more](GNS123_U4_T7#GNS123_U4_T7_h3)

question: When setting priorities during the planning phase, which condition should the nurse address first?

options.A: Risk for impaired skin integrity
options.B: Ineffective airway clearance
options.C: Mild situational anxiety
options.D: Deficient knowledge regarding diet

explanation: Using the ABC (Airway, Breathing, Circulation) priority framework, an airway issue is immediately life-threatening and takes precedence over all other choices. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T7#GNS123_U4_T7_h4)

question: Which of the following represents a properly formulated SMART expected outcome?

options.A: The patient will feel better by tomorrow.
options.B: The nurse will walk the patient twice a shift.
options.C: The patient will ambulate 30 meters in the hallway unassisted by end of day.
options.D: The patient's blood pressure will return to normal eventually.

explanation: This outcome is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound (with a clear timeframe and specific criteria). [learn more](GNS123_U4_T7#GNS123_U4_T7_h4)

question: Which of the following is an example of an independent nursing intervention?

options.A: Administering prescribed intravenous antibiotics
options.B: Ordering a complete blood count lab test
options.C: Repositioning a bedridden patient every two hours to prevent pressure ulcers
options.D: Prescribing a therapeutic diet for a diabetic patient

explanation: Repositioning is an autonomous nursing action that does not require a physician's order, making it an independent intervention. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T7#GNS123_U4_T7_h5)

question: What type of nursing intervention requires a formal order from a licensed medical provider?

options.A: Independent intervention
options.B: Dependent intervention
options.C: Collaborative intervention
options.D: Autonomous intervention

explanation: Dependent interventions rely on orders or supervision from physicians, nurse practitioners, or other authorized medical providers. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T7#GNS123_U4_T7_h5)

question: What is the primary action performed by the nurse during the evaluation phase?

options.A: Comparing the patient's actual outcomes with the expected outcomes
options.B: Gathering baseline subjective data upon patient admission
options.C: Writing new medical diagnoses in the patient chart
options.D: Administering emergency medications for acute pain

explanation: Evaluation centers on measuring the patient's progress by comparing actual results against the goals established in the planning phase. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T7#GNS123_U4_T7_h6)

question: What should a nurse do if an expected outcome is determined to be unmet during evaluation?

options.A: Discharge the patient immediately
options.B: Ignore the outcome and close the nursing chart
options.C: Reassess, analyze the contributing factors, and revise the care plan
options.D: Blame other healthcare team members for the failure

explanation: When goals are unmet, the nurse must re-examine the assessment, diagnosis, and interventions, and modify the care plan as needed. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T7#GNS123_U4_T7_h6)

question: How is clinical reasoning best defined in the context of nursing practice?

options.A: The physical ability to perform bedside nursing procedures quickly
options.B: The mental process used to analyze clinical issues, make inferences, and determine patient actions
options.C: The rote memorization of pharmacology drug classifications
options.D: The administrative task of completing daily shift reports

explanation: Clinical reasoning is the cognitive process nurses use to think through patient situations and decide on safe, appropriate actions. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T7#GNS123_U4_T7_h7)

question: Why are critical thinking and clinical reasoning essential for nursing students?

options.A: They allow nurses to bypass the assessment phase entirely.
options.B: They enable nurses to analyze complex data, anticipate complications, and make sound clinical decisions.
options.C: They eliminate all documentation requirements in the hospital.
options.D: They replace the need for collaboration with physicians.

explanation: Critical thinking helps nurses process complex information and anticipate patient changes, leading to safer and more effective clinical interventions. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T7#GNS123_U4_T7_h7)

question: What does the acronym SBAR stand for in nursing communication?

options.A: Symptoms, Background, Assessment, Recovery
options.B: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation
options.C: Safety, Behavior, Analysis, Response
options.D: Subjective, Baseline, Action, Re-evaluation

explanation: SBAR stands for Situation, Background, Assessment, and Recommendation, providing a standardized framework for safe clinical handoffs. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T7#GNS123_U4_T7_h8)

question: Why is accurate and timely nursing documentation legally and clinically important?

options.A: It serves as a permanent legal record of care and ensures continuity across multidisciplinary teams.
options.B: It replaces the need for verbal shift handoff reports.
options.C: It is only required for billing and hospital insurance purposes.
options.D: It allows nurses to avoid evaluating patient outcomes.

explanation: Proper documentation provides a legal defense and guarantees that all healthcare team members are informed about ongoing patient care. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T7#GNS123_U4_T7_h8)

question: What is the primary purpose of a unidirectional workflow in the operating room environment?

options.A: To speed up the movement of surgical instruments
options.B: To prevent cross-contamination between clean and contaminated areas
options.C: To ensure patients spend less time in the surgical suite
options.D: To reduce the electricity consumption of the surgical lights

explanation: A unidirectional workflow organizes the movement of staff, patients, and supplies to prevent cross-contamination and maintain safety. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T1#GNS123_U5_T1_h1)

question: Why are operating room walls, floors, and ceilings designed with non-porous surfaces?

options.A: To withstand frequent and rigorous disinfection
options.B: To improve the acoustic quality for music playing
options.C: To reflect maximum light into the surgical wound
options.D: To lower the cost of initial facility construction

explanation: Non-porous surfaces are used because they do not absorb moisture and can withstand rigorous cleaning and disinfection. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T1#GNS123_U5_T1_h1)

question: Which operating theatre zone permits the wearing of ordinary street clothes?

options.A: Restricted area
options.B: Semi-restricted area
options.C: Unrestricted area
options.D: Scrub sink alcove

explanation: The unrestricted area acts as a transition zone where street clothes are permitted before entering the scrub and changing areas. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T1#GNS123_U5_T1_h2)

question: What attire is mandatory when entering the semi-restricted area of the surgical suite?

options.A: Complete sterile surgical gown and gloves
options.B: Surgical scrubs, dedicated footwear, and hair covers
options.C: Ordinary street clothes with a lab coat
options.D: Heavy lead aprons and sterile shoe covers

explanation: Personnel in the semi-restricted area must wear surgical scrubs, dedicated footwear, and hair covers to minimize contaminants. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T1#GNS123_U5_T1_h2)

question: What type of air pressure is maintained inside the operating room relative to the surrounding corridors?

options.A: Negative pressure
options.B: Positive pressure
options.C: Neutral atmospheric pressure
options.D: Fluctuating variable pressure

explanation: Positive pressure ensures air flows outward from the OR into corridors, preventing contaminated air from entering the sterile space. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T1#GNS123_U5_T1_h3)

question: What is the primary function of HEPA filters in the operating room HVAC system?

options.A: To humidify the dry air entering the surgical suite
options.B: To remove microscopic particles, dust, and airborne microorganisms
options.C: To cool down the surgical lights during long procedures
options.D: To increase the concentration of oxygen in the room

explanation: HEPA filters are designed to capture microscopic particles, dust, and airborne microorganisms to maintain high air purity. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T1#GNS123_U5_T1_h3)

question: Why must an operating table often be radiolucent during certain procedures?

options.A: To prevent electrical shocks from the electrosurgical unit
options.B: To allow intraoperative imaging such as X-rays to pass through
options.C: To keep the patient warm during long surgeries
options.D: to repel airborne dust particles from settling

explanation: Radiolucent operating tables allow imaging equipment like X-ray machines to capture images without obstruction from the table material. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T1#GNS123_U5_T1_h4)

question: What is a crucial safety precaution when using an electrosurgical unit (diathermy) in the OR?

options.A: Ensuring the correct placement of the patient grounding pad
options.B: Turning off all overhead surgical lights
options.C: Connecting the unit to a portable oxygen cylinder
options.D: Using ungrounded power outlets for the device

explanation: Correct placement of the patient grounding pad prevents electrical current from causing patient burns during electrosurgery. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T1#GNS123_U5_T1_h4)

question: What action should be taken if there is any doubt about the sterility of an item in the operating room?

options.A: Wipe it down with alcohol and use it immediately
options.B: Assume it is contaminated and discard or re-sterilize it
options.C: Ask the surgeon if it looks safe to use
options.D: Place it on the edge of the sterile field

explanation: If there is any doubt regarding the sterility of an item, it must be considered contaminated and discarded to protect the patient. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T1#GNS123_U5_T1_h5)

question: How should sterile team members pass each other within the sterile area to maintain sterility?

options.A: Back-to-back or face-to-face
options.B: Side-to-side with arms touching
options.C: Facing away from each other
options.D: Underneath the instrument table

explanation: Sterile personnel should always pass back-to-back or face-to-face to avoid accidental contamination of sterile gowns. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T1#GNS123_U5_T1_h5)

question: What three elements make up the surgical fire triad present in many operating rooms?

options.A: Water, electricity, and ventilation
options.B: Ignition source, oxidizer, and fuel
options.C: Anesthetic gas, sterile drape, and patient blood
options.D: Surgeon, nurse, and patient

explanation: A surgical fire requires an ignition source, an oxidizer (like oxygen), and fuel (like drapes) to occur simultaneously. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T1#GNS123_U5_T1_h6)

question: Which medication is critical for the immediate emergency treatment of malignant hyperthermia in the OR?

options.A: Adrenaline
options.B: Atropine
options.C: Dantrolene
options.D: Heparin

explanation: Dantrolene is the specific muscle relaxant and antidote used to treat life-threatening malignant hyperthermia crises. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T1#GNS123_U5_T1_h6)

question: What is the primary role of the scrub nurse within the operating room?

options.A: Managing the non-sterile environment and documentation
options.B: Operating within the sterile field to handle instruments and assist the surgeon
options.C: Administering general anesthesia to the patient
options.D: Transporting the patient to and from the recovery ward

explanation: The scrub nurse works in the sterile field, handing instruments to the surgeon and keeping track of counts. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T1#GNS123_U5_T1_h7)

question: Which team member functions in a non-sterile role outside the sterile boundary to coordinate the overall OR environment?

options.A: The lead surgeon
options.B: The scrub nurse
options.C: The circulating nurse
options.D: The surgical assistant

explanation: The circulating nurse works outside the sterile field to monitor the environment, document care, and coordinate communication. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T1#GNS123_U5_T1_h7)

question: What are the three distinct phases that make up the peri-operative continuum?

options.A: Assessment, implementation, and evaluation
options.B: Pre-operative, intra-operative, and post-operative
options.C: Admission, surgery, and discharge
options.D: Preparation, execution, and recovery

explanation: The peri-operative continuum is traditionally divided into the pre-operative, intra-operative, and post-operative phases. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T10#GNS123_U5_T10_h1)

question: Which regulatory body sets the standards for nursing practice in Nigeria mentioned in the text?

options.A: Medical and Dental Council of Nigeria
options.B: Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria
options.C: Federal Ministry of Health
options.D: National Association of Nigerian Nurses and Midwives

explanation: Nigerian nursing students must meet the standards set by the Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria (NMCN). [learn more](GNS123_U5_T10#GNS123_U5_T10_h1)

question: When does the pre-operative phase officially begin and end?

options.A: From admission to the ward until discharge home
options.B: From the decision for surgery until transfer to the operating room table
options.C: From administration of anesthesia until closure of the surgical wound
options.D: From entry into the recovery room until full functional recovery

explanation: The pre-operative phase starts when the decision for surgery is made and ends when the patient is transferred to the operating table. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T10#GNS123_U5_T10_h2)

question: What is the primary role of the nurse regarding informed consent?

options.A: To explain the surgical risks and benefits to the patient
options.B: To sign the consent form on behalf of the unconscious patient
options.C: To verify that the form is signed voluntarily and act as a witness
options.D: To decide whether the patient actually needs the surgery

explanation: The nurse ensures the consent is signed voluntarily and acts as a witness to the patient's signature, while explanation of risks remains the surgeon's duty. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T10#GNS123_U5_T10_h2)

question: Which of the following describes the role of the circulating nurse?

options.A: Wears sterile gown and gloves to hand instruments directly to the surgeon
options.B: Remains non-sterile to manage the overall room environment and document events
options.C: Administers the general anesthesia to the patient during the procedure
options.D: Sutures the surgical skin incision at the end of the operation

explanation: The circulating nurse is non-sterile and manages the operating room environment, coordinates activities, and handles documentation. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T10#GNS123_U5_T10_h3)

question: What is the primary purpose of performing a surgical time-out in the operating room?

options.A: To allow the surgical team to take a coffee break
options.B: To calculate the exact duration of the surgical procedure
options.C: To prevent wrong-site, wrong-procedure, and wrong-person surgeries
options.D: To check the expiration dates of all sterile packaging

explanation: A surgical time-out is a crucial safety verification step used to prevent wrong-site, wrong-procedure, and wrong-person errors. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T10#GNS123_U5_T10_h3)

question: Where is the patient typically cared for immediately following the intra-operative phase?

options.A: In the general outpatient clinic
options.B: In the Post-Anesthesia Care Unit (PACU)
options.C: At home with family members
options.D: In the hospital pharmacy

explanation: Immediately after surgery, the patient is admitted to the PACU for close monitoring of vital signs and airway management. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T10#GNS123_U5_T10_h4)

question: When should discharge planning and education ideally begin for a surgical patient?

options.A: Only after the surgical stitches are removed
options.B: Early in the peri-operative process
options.C: At the exact moment of hospital discharge
options.D: During the patient's first follow-up clinic visit

explanation: Discharge planning should begin early in the peri-operative process to ensure adequate preparation of the patient and family. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T10#GNS123_U5_T10_h4)

question: Why is the nurse's advocacy role particularly critical during the peri-operative period?

options.A: Patients are often vulnerable, unresponsive, or heavily medicated
options.B: Nurses are legally required to perform the actual surgery
options.C: Surgeons do not have time to speak with the patients
options.D: Hospital administrators mandate advocacy over patient care

explanation: Patients are often vulnerable, unresponsive, or medicated during surgery, making nurse advocacy vital for protecting their rights and safety. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T10#GNS123_U5_T10_h5)

question: Which nursing action directly helps prevent retained surgical items?

options.A: Checking the patient's blood pressure every fifteen minutes
options.B: Conducting meticulous and accurate sponge, needle, and instrument counts
options.C: Administering prescribed prophylactic antibiotics on schedule
options.D: Documenting the patient's religious preferences in the chart

explanation: Meticulous and accurate counts of sponges, needles, and instruments by the surgical team prevent retained surgical items. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T10#GNS123_U5_T10_h5)

question: What key characteristic should nursing documentation possess in the peri-operative setting?

options.A: Subjective, speculative, and written days after the event
options.B: Accurate, objective, timely, and contemporaneous
options.C: Filled with personal opinions and emotional commentary
options.D: Completed exclusively by the attending surgeon

explanation: Nursing documentation must be accurate, objective, timely, and contemporaneous to serve as a reliable clinical and legal record. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T10#GNS123_U5_T10_h6)

question: Which ethical principle obligates the nurse to 'do no harm' to the surgical patient?

options.A: Autonomy
options.B: Beneficence
options.C: Non-maleficence
options.D: Justice

explanation: Non-maleficence is the ethical principle that obligates healthcare providers to do no harm to their patients. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T10#GNS123_U5_T10_h6)

question: What is a primary role of the nurse in preventing complications in a medical-surgical ward?

options.A: Discharging patients as quickly as possible
options.B: Identifying subtle clinical changes and implementing proactive measures
options.C: Prescribing alternative pharmacological treatments
options.D: Limiting family involvement in patient care

explanation: Nurses are on the frontline and play a critical role in identifying subtle clinical changes and applying proactive measures to mitigate potential adverse events. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T11#GNS123_U5_T11_h1)

question: Why is the prevention of hospital complications considered essential in nursing practice?

options.A: It eliminates the need for any documentation
options.B: It reduces hospital stays, costs, morbidity, and mortality
options.C: It shifts all medical responsibilities entirely to the patient
options.D: It prevents the need for physical assessments

explanation: Preventing secondary health issues helps shorten hospital stays, lowers costs, and significantly reduces morbidity and mortality rates. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T11#GNS123_U5_T11_h1)

question: Which of the following represents an environment- or treatment-related risk factor for hospital-acquired complications?

options.A: Advanced age
options.B: Pre-existing diabetes mellitus
options.C: Use of indwelling urinary catheters
options.D: Compromised immune function

explanation: The use of invasive devices such as indwelling urinary catheters is a treatment-related risk factor for complications like infections. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T11#GNS123_U5_T11_h2)

question: How does prolonged recumbency primarily contribute to hospital-acquired complications?

options.A: By enhancing physical mobility and strength
options.B: By causing venous stasis, atelectasis, and tissue ischemia
options.C: By immediately curing chronic cardiovascular diseases
options.D: By boosting the patient's immune system

explanation: Prolonged recumbency leads to venous stasis, atelectasis, and pressure-induced tissue ischemia, creating conditions for thrombosis, pneumonia, and pressure injuries. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T11#GNS123_U5_T11_h2)

question: What is the primary purpose of Early Warning Systems (EWS) in nursing practice?

options.A: To replace the need for physical head-to-toe assessments
options.B: To detect physiological deterioration before a catastrophic event occurs
options.C: To calculate the exact cost of hospitalization
options.D: To automatically discharge stable patients

explanation: Early Warning Systems track vital sign deviations to help nurses detect physiological deterioration hours before a major crisis happens. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T11#GNS123_U5_T11_h3)

question: Which parameters are typically evaluated when utilizing a scoring tool like the Modified Early Warning Score (MEWS)?

options.A: Patient occupation and insurance status
options.B: Vital signs and level of consciousness
options.C: Dietary preferences and fluid balance history from childhood
options.D: Family medical history and housing conditions

explanation: MEWS tracks vital signs such as heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, temperature, and level of consciousness. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T11#GNS123_U5_T11_h3)

question: Which of the following is a primary cardiovascular risk associated with prolonged patient immobility?

options.A: Hypertension and tachycardia
options.B: Venous stasis and deep vein thrombosis
options.C: Enhanced peripheral circulation
options.D: Spontaneous vasoconstriction

explanation: Prolonged immobility causes venous stasis, which greatly elevates the risk of deep vein thrombosis and subsequent pulmonary embolism. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T11#GNS123_U5_T11_h4)

question: What is an effective nursing intervention to prevent respiratory complications in immobile patients?

options.A: Restricting fluid intake to prevent fluid overload
options.B: Encouraging deep breathing exercises and incentive spirometry
options.C: Keeping the patient flat in bed for 24 hours a day
options.D: Avoiding any position changes to minimize fatigue

explanation: Encouraging deep breathing and incentive spirometry helps prevent atelectasis and the pooling of respiratory secretions in immobile patients. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T11#GNS123_U5_T11_h4)

question: What is considered the single most effective intervention in preventing the transmission of healthcare-associated infections?

options.A: Prophylactic administration of broad-spectrum antibiotics
options.B: Meticulous hand hygiene by healthcare workers
options.C: Restricting all visitors from entering the hospital ward
options.D: Daily painting of hospital walls with antiseptic solution

explanation: The hands of healthcare workers are the primary vehicle for pathogen transmission, making hand hygiene the most effective preventive measure. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T11#GNS123_U5_T11_h5)

question: When is strict aseptic technique required by a nurse in a medical-surgical setting?

options.A: During routine oral hygiene and feeding assistance
options.B: During invasive procedures such as dressing changes and catheter insertions
options.C: Only when visiting patients in the intensive care unit
options.D: During general bedside conversation and vital sign checks

explanation: Aseptic technique is mandatory during invasive procedures like dressing changes and catheter insertions to prevent introduction of pathogens. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T11#GNS123_U5_T11_h5)

question: What is considered a reliable clinical proxy for adequate systemic organ perfusion in a monitored patient?

options.A: Hourly urine output measurement
options.B: Frequency of bowel movements
options.C: Skin color of the lower extremities alone
options.D: Patient appetite and meal tolerance

explanation: Urine output is widely used by nurses as a direct proxy to evaluate renal and systemic organ perfusion. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T11#GNS123_U5_T11_h6)

question: A sudden drop in blood pressure accompanied by falling urine output most likely suggests what clinical condition?

options.A: Fluid overload and hypertension
options.B: Impending shock (such as hypovolemic or septic)
options.C: Normal physiological sleep cycle
options.D: Hyperactive neurological status

explanation: Falling blood pressure and reduced urine output are classic early signs of inadequate tissue perfusion and impending shock. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T11#GNS123_U5_T11_h6)

question: Which of the following describes a recommended safety practice when administering high-alert medications like insulin or anticoagulants?

options.A: Administering the medication without checking patient ID bands to save time
options.B: Performing an independent double-check with a second nurse
options.C: Ignoring patient allergies if the physician ordered the drug
options.D: Skipping documentation to expedite medication rounds

explanation: High-alert medications require an independent double-check by a second nurse to reduce the risk of calculation and administration errors. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T11#GNS123_U5_T11_h7)

question: What is a primary responsibility of the nurse after administering a medication?

options.A: Assuming the drug is safe and walking away without further observation
options.B: Monitoring the patient for both therapeutic effects and adverse reactions
options.C: Immediately discharging the patient to clear the bed
options.D: Prescribing the next dose adjustment independently

explanation: Nurses must actively observe patients after medication administration to evaluate therapeutic outcomes and catch adverse drug reactions early. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T11#GNS123_U5_T11_h7)

question: What does the acronym SBAR stand for in the context of interprofessional communication?

options.A: Safety, Breathing, Assessment, Recovery
options.B: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation
options.C: System, Blood-pressure, Action, Rate
options.D: Symptoms, Bedside, Analysis, Response

explanation: SBAR stands for Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation, providing a structured format for clear clinical communication. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T11#GNS123_U5_T11_h8)

question: What is the primary function of a Rapid Response System (RRS) or Medical Emergency Team (MET) in a hospital?

options.A: To handle routine administrative patient admissions
options.B: To summon immediate critical care expertise at the earliest sign of patient deterioration
options.C: To conduct annual hospital facility inspections
options.D: To replace standard nursing vital sign charting

explanation: Rapid Response Systems allow staff to bring critical care expertise directly to the bedside early, preventing severe adverse events. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T11#GNS123_U5_T11_h8)

question: What is one of the primary reasons the operating room environment is considered uniquely hazardous for nurses?

options.A: It involves low-stress, routine tasks with minimal equipment.
options.B: It features a confined space with high-stakes procedures and specialized equipment.
options.C: Nurses spend most of their shift sitting down away from patients.
options.D: There is a complete absence of chemical and biological substances.

explanation: The OR is a confined space featuring specialized equipment, high-stress procedures, and vulnerable patients, which increases the exposure to various occupational risks. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T12#GNS123_U5_T12_h1)

question: Why is studying operating room hazards important for nursing students?

options.A: To encourage them to avoid working in surgical departments entirely
options.B: To promote a safety-first mindset and strict adherence to universal precautions
options.C: To focus solely on patient safety while ignoring personal health
options.D: To eliminate the need for institutional safety policies

explanation: Recognizing hazards helps students develop a safety-first mindset and appreciate the importance of universal precautions and safety guidelines in the theater. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T12#GNS123_U5_T12_h1)

question: Which of the following is a common physical hazard resulting from prolonged standing and heavy lifting in the OR?

options.A: Musculoskeletal disorders and chronic lower back pain
options.B: Chemical burns from antiseptic solutions
options.C: Bacterial sepsis from contaminated wounds
options.D: Psychological burnout from administrative meetings

explanation: Prolonged standing, awkward postures, and heavy lifting frequently cause musculoskeletal disorders and chronic lower back pain among OR nurses. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T12#GNS123_U5_T12_h2)

question: How can operating room nurses best protect themselves against radiation exposure from C-arm fluoroscopy machines?

options.A: By wearing sterile gloves and surgical masks
options.B: By utilizing lead aprons, thyroid collars, and distance barriers
options.C: By turning off all operating room lights during imaging
options.D: By increasing the volume of surgical equipment alarms

explanation: Proper protective gear like lead aprons and thyroid collars, alongside maintaining distance, are essential to shield against radiation exposure. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T12#GNS123_U5_T12_h2)

question: Which bloodborne infections are of primary concern following a needle-stick injury in the operating room?

options.A: Malaria and typhoid fever
options.B: Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and HIV
options.C: Tuberculosis and cholera
options.D: Tetanus and pneumonia

question: What is surgical smoke plume and why is it dangerous?

options.A: It is harmless steam created by boiling sterile water instruments.

options.C: It is dust kicked up from ventilation systems during floor cleaning.
options.D: It is carbon dioxide gas used exclusively for laparoscopic insufflation.

explanation: Surgical smoke plume is generated by energy devices and contains hazardous chemicals, viable bacteria, and viral particles that pose respiratory risks when inhaled. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T12#GNS123_U5_T12_h3)

question: What potential health issue is associated with chronic, low-level exposure to leaked anesthetic gases in the OR?

options.A: Chronic headaches, drowsiness, and reproductive issues
options.B: Immediate bone fractures and joint swelling
options.C: Bacterial wound infections and sepsis
options.D: Total permanent hearing loss

question: Why is the combination of alcohol-based skin preps and oxygen-rich environments dangerous in the OR?

options.A: It neutralizes the effectiveness of the antiseptic.

options.C: It causes immediate respiratory paralysis in the patient.
options.D: It stains surgical linen permanently.

explanation: Flammable agents like alcohol preps combined with oxygen-rich atmospheres create high fire risks when exposed to electrosurgical ignition sources. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T12#GNS123_U5_T12_h4)

question: What is a major contributor to psychological distress and trauma in operating room nurses?

options.A: Managing life-threatening surgical emergencies and witnessing patient mortality
options.B: Spending too much time on paperwork in administrative offices
options.C: A lack of physical equipment in the surgical supply room
options.D: Having too many scheduled breaks during a shift

explanation: Managing critical emergencies, massive hemorrhages, and witnessing patient mortality are key sources of intense psychological stress and trauma in the OR. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T12#GNS123_U5_T12_h5)

question: How does occupational burnout primarily affect a perioperative nurse?

options.A: By increasing physical height and muscle mass
options.B: Through emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and compromised patient safety
options.C: By making them immune to biological and chemical hazards
options.D: By eliminating the need for personal protective equipment

explanation: Burnout involves emotional exhaustion and depersonalization, which negatively affects the nurse's well-being and can jeopardize patient safety. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T12#GNS123_U5_T12_h5)

question: How can hierarchical intimidation and incivility in the operating room negatively impact patient care?

options.A: By speeding up surgical procedures unnecessarily
options.B: By causing junior staff and students to hesitate in reporting critical safety concerns
options.C: By improving the overall sterile technique of the surgical team
options.D: By reducing the cost of surgical instruments

explanation: Intimidation creates fear, causing junior nurses and students to withhold vital safety warnings, which leads to preventable medical errors. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T12#GNS123_U5_T12_h6)

question: What is a key requirement for overcoming social and communication barriers in the surgical suite?

options.A: Enforcing strict isolation between different medical professions
options.B: Cultivating a culture of psychological safety and empowering staff to voice concerns
options.C: Removing all nursing staff from surgical decision-making processes
options.D: Eliminating surgical checklists to save time

explanation: Psychological safety ensures that all team members feel respected and empowered to communicate openly, enhancing both teamwork and patient safety. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T12#GNS123_U5_T12_h6)

question: What is a major legal hazard in perioperative nursing that can lead to malpractice claims and regulatory disciplinary action?

options.A: Failing to wear colorful scrubs in the theater

options.C: Arriving five minutes early for a surgical shift
options.D: Participating in interprofessional team meetings

explanation: Retained surgical items are severe, preventable errors that expose nurses to major malpractice liabilities and disciplinary actions. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T12#GNS123_U5_T12_h7)

question: What serves as an operating room nurse's strongest legal defense in the event of a malpractice allegation?

options.A: Accurate, meticulous, and contemporaneous documentation of all care
options.B: Verbal agreements made with the surgical team
options.C: Memory recall of events several months after surgery
options.D: Blaming other members of the multidisciplinary team

explanation: Thorough, accurate, and timely documentation provides concrete evidence of standard nursing care delivered during the procedure. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T12#GNS123_U5_T12_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of implementing the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist in the operating room?

options.A: To increase the duration and complexity of surgical procedures

options.C: To evaluate the financial budget of the hospital department
options.D: To replace the need for physical and chemical hazard training

explanation: The WHO checklist mandates crucial safety pauses to verify patient identity, surgical site, and counts, significantly reducing preventable errors. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T12#GNS123_U5_T12_h8)

question: Which occupational health service is essential following a needle-stick injury in the operating room?

options.A: Immediate disciplinary suspension of the nurse
