question: Why is inter-sectoral collaboration crucial for long-term rehabilitation success?

options.A: It prevents medical professionals from interacting with social workers
options.B: It ensures that medical recovery is supported by accessible environments, employment, and education
options.C: It increases bureaucratic delays across government ministries
options.D: It reduces the need for assistive devices and therapy

explanation: Collaboration ensures medical recovery is not undermined by inaccessible environments, lack of transport, or absence of vocational opportunities, supporting holistic needs. [learn more](GNS123_U6_T6#GNS123_U6_T6_h7)

question: What is the primary mechanical role of the heart within the cardiovascular system?

options.A: To filter metabolic waste products
options.B: To act as a pump distributing blood
options.C: To synthesize clotting factors
options.D: To regulate core body pH exclusively

explanation: The heart functions as a muscular pump that drives blood throughout the entire vascular network to deliver vital substances. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T1#GNS213_U1_T1_h1)

question: Which of the following is transported away from tissues by the cardiovascular system for elimination?

options.A: Oxygen
options.B: Glucose
options.C: Carbon dioxide
options.D: Hormones

explanation: Metabolic byproducts like carbon dioxide are collected by the cardiovascular system and transported to the lungs for elimination from the body. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T1#GNS213_U1_T1_h1)

question: Which layer of the heart wall is the thickest and responsible for the pumping action?

options.A: Epicardium
options.B: Endocardium
options.C: Myocardium
options.D: Pericardium

explanation: The myocardium is composed of cardiac muscle tissue and forms the thick middle layer responsible for generating the force needed to pump blood. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T1#GNS213_U1_T1_h2)

question: What is the primary function of the endocardium?

options.A: To secrete lubricating pericardial fluid
options.B: To line the heart chambers and prevent abnormal clotting
options.C: To provide a fibrous outer protective covering
options.D: To anchor the heart within the mediastinum

explanation: The endocardium is a smooth endothelial lining that covers the heart chambers and valves to ensure blood flows smoothly without inappropriate clotting. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T1#GNS213_U1_T1_h2)

question: Which valve separates the right atrium from the right ventricle?

options.A: Mitral valve
options.B: Aortic valve
options.C: Tricuspid valve
options.D: Pulmonary valve

explanation: The tricuspid valve is the atrioventricular valve located between the right atrium and the right ventricle. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T1#GNS213_U1_T1_h3)

question: What is the primary function of the chordae tendineae and papillary muscles?

options.A: To open the semilunar valves during systole
options.B: To prevent the AV valves from prolapsing into the atria
options.C: To generate the electrical impulse for heart contraction
options.D: To pump blood directly into the coronary circulation

explanation: Chordae tendineae and papillary muscles anchor the AV valve flaps to prevent them from blowing backward into the atria when the ventricles contract. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T1#GNS213_U1_T1_h3)

question: When does the majority of coronary blood flow to the myocardium occur?

options.A: During ventricular systole
options.B: During atrial systole
options.C: During ventricular diastole
options.D: During isovolumetric contraction

explanation: Coronary vessels are compressed during systole, so most myocardial perfusion takes place during ventricular diastole when the heart muscle relaxes. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T1#GNS213_U1_T1_h4)

question: Where do the coronary arteries originate?

options.A: The superior vena cava
options.B: The base of the ascending aorta
options.C: The pulmonary trunk
options.D: The right atrium

explanation: The right and left coronary arteries branch directly off the base of the ascending aorta, immediately above the aortic semilunar valve. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T1#GNS213_U1_T1_h4)

question: Which structure serves as the primary natural pacemaker of the heart?

options.A: AV node
options.B: SA node
options.C: Bundle of His
options.D: Purkinje fibers

explanation: The sinoatrial (SA) node has the highest rate of spontaneous depolarization, making it the primary pacemaker that sets the heart rate. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T1#GNS213_U1_T1_h5)

question: What is the physiological significance of the delay at the AV node?

options.A: It prevents the atria from ever contracting
options.B: It allows the ventricles time to fill completely with blood
options.C: It speeds up the electrical signal to the Purkinje fibers
options.D: It initiates the repolarization of the T wave

explanation: The brief delay at the AV node ensures that the atria finish contracting and emptying their blood into the ventricles before ventricular systole begins. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T1#GNS213_U1_T1_h5)

question: What event directly causes the first heart sound (S1, or 'lub')?

options.A: Opening of the semilunar valves
options.B: Closure of the atrioventricular valves
options.C: Opening of the atrioventricular valves
options.D: Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves

explanation: The first heart sound (S1) is produced by the sudden snapping shut of the mitral and tricuspid (AV) valves at the beginning of ventricular systole. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T1#GNS213_U1_T1_h6)

question: During which phase of the cardiac cycle do the ventricles contract with all valves closed, causing pressure to rise without volume change?

options.A: Ventricular ejection
options.B: Isovolumetric relaxation
options.C: Ventricular filling
options.D: Isovolumetric contraction

explanation: Isovolumetric contraction occurs when the ventricles start contracting with all four valves closed, causing pressure to spike without any change in blood volume. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T1#GNS213_U1_T1_h6)

question: How is cardiac output (CO) calculated?

options.A: Stroke volume divided by heart rate
options.B: Heart rate multiplied by stroke volume
options.C: Blood pressure divided by resistance
options.D: Preload multiplied by afterload

explanation: Cardiac output is the volume of blood pumped per minute, calculated as heart rate times stroke volume (CO = HR x SV). [learn more](GNS213_U1_T1#GNS213_U1_T1_h7)

question: What does the Frank-Starling law of the heart relate to preload?

options.A: Increased stretch of muscle fibers leads to a stronger contraction
options.B: Higher arterial resistance decreases the stroke volume
options.C: Faster heart rate decreases the filling time
options.D: Vasoconstriction increases systemic vascular resistance

explanation: The Frank-Starling law explains that greater filling (preload) stretches cardiomyocytes, leading to a more forceful contraction and increased stroke volume. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T1#GNS213_U1_T1_h7)

question: Which blood vessels act as the primary resistance vessels that regulate systemic blood pressure?

options.A: Capillaries
options.B: Arterioles
options.C: Large elastic arteries
options.D: Venules

explanation: Arterioles possess significant smooth muscle in their walls, allowing them to constrict or dilate to control blood flow and resistance into capillary beds. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T1#GNS213_U1_T1_h8)

question: What structural feature do medium and large veins possess to prevent the backward flow of blood against gravity?

options.A: Thick elastic muscular walls
options.B: One-way valves
options.C: Single-layered endothelial walls
options.D: Precapillary sphincters

explanation: Veins feature one-way valves that work alongside skeletal muscle contractions to push low-pressure blood upward toward the heart without backflow. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T1#GNS213_U1_T1_h8)

question: Which blood vessels are primarily responsible for regulating systemic blood pressure through vasoconstriction and vasodilation before blood reaches the capillaries?

options.A: Vena cava
options.B: Arterioles
options.C: Venules
options.D: Capillaries

explanation: Arterioles branch out from arteries and play a critical role in regulating systemic blood pressure through vasoconstriction and vasodilation before transitioning into capillaries. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T10#GNS213_U1_T10_h1)

question: What structural feature do veins possess to help return deoxygenated blood to the heart against gravity?

options.A: Thick muscular walls
options.B: High systolic elasticity
options.C: One-way valves
options.D: Microscopic pores

explanation: Veins feature one-way valves that prevent the backflow of blood as it travels upward against gravity back to the heart. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T10#GNS213_U1_T10_h1)

question: What primary event initiates the development of atherosclerosis in the arterial wall?

options.A: Endothelial injury
options.B: Venous valve failure
options.C: Capillary proliferation
options.D: Arterial vasodilation

explanation: Atherosclerosis begins with endothelial injury caused by risk factors like hypertension, smoking, and hyperlipidemia, leading to lipid accumulation and plaque formation. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T10#GNS213_U1_T10_h2)

question: How does vasospasm differ structurally from atherosclerosis?

options.A: It involves permanent deposition of calcium in the intima.
options.B: It is a functional disorder involving sudden contraction of arterial smooth muscle without fixed plaques.
options.C: It exclusively affects large capacitance veins rather than arteries.
options.D: It results from chronic inflammation and foam cell death.

explanation: Vasospasm is a functional disorder characterized by sudden, involuntary constriction of arterial smooth muscle that drastically reduces blood flow, often without fixed atherosclerotic plaques. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T10#GNS213_U1_T10_h2)

question: What is the hallmark symptom of chronic Peripheral Arterial Disease (PAD)?

options.A: Pitting edema in the lower ankles
options.B: Intermittent claudication relieved by rest
options.C: Warm, erythematous lower extremities
options.D: Sudden paralysis with no pain

explanation: Intermittent claudication is the classic hallmark symptom of chronic PAD, presenting as ischemic muscle pain during exertion that subsides with rest. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T10#GNS213_U1_T10_h3)

question: Which of the following clinical manifestations represents part of the '6 Ps' of acute arterial occlusion?

options.A: Bounding peripheral pulses
options.B: Flushed, warm skin
options.C: Poikilothermia
options.D: Dependent rubor with edema

explanation: Poikilothermia, or coolness of the affected extremity, is one of the classic '6 Ps' indicating acute arterial occlusion and lack of blood flow. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T10#GNS213_U1_T10_h3)

question: What is the primary underlying cause of both varicose veins and chronic venous insufficiency?

options.A: Atherosclerotic plaque accumulation in arteries
options.B: Incompetent venous valves and weakened vein walls
options.C: Arterial vasospasm triggered by cold exposure
options.D: Excessive production of red blood cells

explanation: Varicose veins and CVI are primarily caused by weakened vein walls and incompetent valves that allow blood to pool, increasing venous pressure. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T10#GNS213_U1_T10_h4)

question: Where are typical venous stasis ulcers associated with chronic venous insufficiency most commonly located?

options.A: Over the medial malleolus
options.B: On the tips of the toes
options.C: On the dorsal surface of the foot
options.D: In the center of the anterior thigh

explanation: Venous stasis ulcers resulting from chronic venous insufficiency are typically located over the medial malleolus of the lower leg. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T10#GNS213_U1_T10_h4)

question: What are the three components of Virchow's triad that contribute to the formation of deep vein thrombosis?

options.A: Vasospasm, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia
options.B: Venous stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability
options.C: Arterial occlusion, inflammation, and plaque rupture
options.D: Valvular incompetence, edema, and ischemia

explanation: Virchow's triad consists of venous stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability, which together increase the risk of thrombosis. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T10#GNS213_U1_T10_h5)

question: Which of the following symptoms is most characteristic of a pulmonary embolism resulting from a dislodged DVT?

options.A: Sudden onset of dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain
options.B: Intermittent claudication in the calf muscles
options.C: Dependent pitting edema in both ankles
options.D: Pulsating mass felt in the abdomen

explanation: Sudden shortness of breath (dyspnea) and pleuritic chest pain are hallmark signs of a pulmonary embolism when a thrombus blocks the pulmonary vasculature. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T10#GNS213_U1_T10_h5)

question: How is an aortic dissection pathologically different from an aortic aneurysm?

options.A: An aneurysm involves a tear in the intima with blood entering the vessel wall layers, whereas dissection is a simple dilation.
options.B: A dissection involves a tear in the intimal layer creating a false lumen, whereas an aneurysm is a balloon-like dilation of the weakened wall.
options.C: An aneurysm only affects peripheral veins, whereas dissection affects coronary arteries.
options.D: A dissection is caused exclusively by atherosclerosis, whereas aneurysms are congenital only.

explanation: An aortic dissection occurs when an intimal tear lets blood flow between the arterial wall layers, whereas an aneurysm is a localized ballooning of the weakened wall. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T10#GNS213_U1_T10_h6)

question: What is the classic description of pain reported by a patient experiencing an acute aortic dissection?

options.A: Dull, aching calf pain relieved by rest
options.B: Cramping abdominal pain after eating
options.C: Sudden 'tearing' or 'ripping' chest or back pain
options.D: Sharp, localized pain in the right lower quadrant

explanation: Patients experiencing an aortic dissection classically describe a sudden, severe 'tearing' or 'ripping' pain radiating to the chest, back, or shoulders. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T10#GNS213_U1_T10_h6)

question: When palpating peripheral pulses, how is an absent pulse typically graded on the standard clinical scale?
explanation: Peripheral pulses are graded on a scale where 0 indicates an absent pulse, while 1+ to 4+ denote diminished to bounding pulses. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T10#GNS213_U1_T10_h7)

question: What is the primary clinical purpose of calculating an Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI)?

options.A: To measure the severity of chronic venous insufficiency
options.B: To evaluate blood pressure differences used to diagnose Peripheral Arterial Disease (PAD)
options.C: To assess the presence of deep vein thrombosis in the calf
options.D: To detect the exact location of an aortic aneurysm

explanation: The ABI compares ankle systolic blood pressure to brachial pressure, serving as a key non-invasive test to diagnose and grade Peripheral Arterial Disease (PAD). [learn more](GNS213_U1_T10#GNS213_U1_T10_h7)

question: Which class of medications is primarily prescribed to patients with Peripheral Arterial Disease to prevent platelet aggregation and thrombotic events?

options.A: Antiplatelets (e.g., aspirin, clopidogrel)
options.B: Thrombolytics (e.g., alteplase)
options.C: Diuretics (e.g., furosemide)
options.D: Vasoconstrictors (e.g., norepinephrine)

explanation: Antiplatelet medications like aspirin and clopidogrel are prescribed to prevent platelets from clumping together, reducing the risk of thrombotic events in arterial disease. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T10#GNS213_U1_T10_h8)

question: What is the main purpose of statin therapy in patients with vascular disease?

options.A: To rapidly dissolve established acute blood clots
options.B: To lower LDL cholesterol and help stabilize atherosclerotic plaques
options.C: To dilate peripheral blood vessels during a vasospasm
options.D: To decrease systemic fluid volume and reduce edema

explanation: Statins are used to lower lipid levels and stabilize atherosclerotic plaques, reducing the risk of plaque rupture and disease progression. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T10#GNS213_U1_T10_h8)

question: How should a nurse instruct a patient with chronic venous insufficiency regarding lower extremity positioning?

options.A: Keep legs dependent below heart level at all times
options.B: Elevate legs above the level of the heart periodically to promote venous return
options.C: Avoid any movement and keep legs flat on the bed
options.D: Apply ice packs directly to the calves to reduce swelling

explanation: Patients with venous insufficiency should elevate their legs above heart level to assist venous return and decrease edema pooling. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T10#GNS213_U1_T10_h9)

question: What is a vital lifestyle modification that a nurse must emphasize to a patient diagnosed with any major vascular disorder?

options.A: Complete cessation of smoking
options.B: Increasing daily dietary sodium intake
options.C: Avoiding all forms of physical activity
options.D: Stopping prescribed medications once symptoms improve

explanation: Smoking causes endothelial injury and vasoconstriction, making strict smoking cessation an essential lifestyle modification for all vascular patients. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T10#GNS213_U1_T10_h9)

question: Which component of the vascular system is primarily responsible for preventing the backflow of blood against gravity?

options.A: Arterioles
options.B: Venous one-way valves
options.C: Capillary beds
options.D: Conduit arteries

explanation: Veins feature one-way valves that prevent the backflow of blood against gravity, relying on skeletal muscle contractions for return flow. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T11#GNS213_U1_T11_h1)

question: What is the primary physiological consequence of alterations in the arterial supply to peripheral tissues?

options.A: Venous congestion
options.B: Edema formation
options.C: Ischemic tissue damage
options.D: Stasis ulceration

explanation: Alterations or blockages in the arterial supply restrict oxygenated blood flow, directly resulting in ischemic tissue damage. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T11#GNS213_U1_T11_h1)

question: What is the initial hallmark cellular event in the development of an atherosclerotic plaque?

options.A: Fibrous cap calcification
options.B: Deposition of low-density lipoproteins in the intimal layer
options.C: Venous valve incompetence
options.D: Massive vasodilation of arterioles

explanation: Atherosclerosis begins with the deposition of low-density lipoproteins (LDL) within the intimal layer of medium and large arteries. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T11#GNS213_U1_T11_h2)

question: What is the primary pathological mechanism underlying chronic venous insufficiency?

options.A: Arterial plaque rupture
options.B: Incompetent venous valves causing ambulatory venous hypertension
options.C: Proliferation of smooth muscle cells in arterioles
options.D: Excess production of nitric oxide by the endothelium

explanation: Chronic venous insufficiency occurs when incompetent venous valves lead to ambulatory venous hypertension and subsequent fluid extravasation. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T11#GNS213_U1_T11_h2)

question: Which of the following is classified as an acute surgical emergency among arterial disorders?

options.A: Peripheral Artery Disease
options.B: Raynaud's phenomenon
options.C: Acute limb ischemia
options.D: Buerger's disease

explanation: Acute limb ischemia is a sudden, severe interruption of arterial blood flow that requires immediate surgical intervention. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T11#GNS213_U1_T11_h3)

question: What is a primary characteristic of Buerger's disease (thromboangiitis obliterans)?

options.A: It is heavily linked to tobacco use and affects small and medium-sized vessels.
options.B: It is caused by incompetent venous valves in the lower extremities.
options.C: It involves episodic arterial vasospasms triggered by cold temperatures only.
options.D: It is an acute embolic event originating from the left atrium.

explanation: Buerger's disease is a non-atherosclerotic, segmental inflammatory condition strongly linked to tobacco use affecting small and medium-sized arteries and veins. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T11#GNS213_U1_T11_h3)

question: Which of the following represents a non-modifiable risk factor for peripheral circulation disorders?

options.A: Cigarette smoking
options.B: Advanced age
options.C: Diabetes mellitus
options.D: Physical inactivity

explanation: Advanced age is a non-modifiable risk factor, whereas smoking, diabetes, and physical inactivity can be changed or managed. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T11#GNS213_U1_T11_h4)

question: How does diabetes mellitus specifically accelerate peripheral arterial disease?

options.A: By causing rapid venous valve incompetence
options.B: Through chronic hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia, and advanced glycation end-products
options.C: By inducing hyper-salivation and localized skin dryness
options.D: Through immediate vasospasm of the digital arteries

explanation: Diabetes mellitus accelerates atherosclerosis and ischemia through chronic hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia, and advanced glycation end-products that damage vessels. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T11#GNS213_U1_T11_h4)

question: What is the defining characteristic of intermittent claudication in peripheral artery disease?

options.A: Pain that occurs at rest and is relieved by walking
options.B: Cramp-like muscle pain triggered by exercise and relieved by rest
options.C: Unilateral limb swelling with pitting edema
options.D: Sharp, throbbing pain that worsens with leg elevation

explanation: Intermittent claudication is a cramp-like pain brought on by physical exertion and promptly relieved by resting the affected muscle group. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T11#GNS213_U1_T11_h5)

question: Which physical assessment finding is most characteristic of chronic venous insufficiency?

options.A: Dependent rubor and absent peripheral pulses
options.B: Punched-out, dry arterial ulcers on the toes
options.C: Brownish skin pigmentation, edema, and a heavy aching sensation
options.D: Cold extremities with pallor upon elevation

explanation: Chronic venous insufficiency typically presents with a heavy, aching sensation, pitting edema, and brownish skin pigmentation from hemosiderin deposition. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T11#GNS213_U1_T11_h5)

question: What Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI) value is typically indicative of peripheral artery disease?

options.B: Above 1.40
options.C: Below 0.90
options.D: Exactly 1.00

explanation: An ABI below 0.90 is the standard diagnostic threshold indicating abnormal arterial blood flow and peripheral artery disease. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T11#GNS213_U1_T11_h6)

question: What is a vital post-procedure nursing responsibility following a diagnostic angiography using contrast dye?

options.A: Restricting all oral fluids to prevent bladder distension
options.B: Ensuring adequate hydration to protect renal function
options.C: Applying hot compresses directly to the vascular access site
options.D: Encouraging immediate heavy exercise to promote circulation

explanation: Ensuring adequate hydration is essential after contrast dye studies to flush the nephrotoxic dye and protect renal function. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T11#GNS213_U1_T11_h6)

question: Which pharmacological agent is specifically prescribed to improve walking distance in patients with intermittent claudication?

options.A: Cilostazol
options.B: Warfarin
options.C: Heparin
options.D: Insulin

explanation: Cilostazol is a phosphodiesterase inhibitor with vasodilator and antiplatelet properties prescribed to improve walking distance in intermittent claudication. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T11#GNS213_U1_T11_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of percutaneous transluminal angioplasty (PTA) in treating peripheral artery disease?

options.A: To bypass the entire diseased vessel using a synthetic graft
options.B: To dissolve deep vein thrombosis using chemical thrombolysis
options.C: To compress atherosclerotic plaque and widen the arterial lumen using a balloon catheter
options.D: To permanently prevent future venous valve incompetence

explanation: PTA involves using a balloon-tipped catheter to mechanically compress atherosclerotic plaque and restore adequate lumen diameter. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T11#GNS213_U1_T11_h7)

question: How should a nurse instruct a patient with chronic venous insufficiency regarding limb positioning?

options.A: Keep legs dependent at all times to encourage arterial filling
options.B: Elevate the legs above the level of the heart to reduce edema
options.C: Cross the legs at the knees while sitting to stabilize venous pressure
options.D: Avoid all movement and remain strictly on bed rest flat

explanation: Patients with venous insufficiency should elevate their legs above heart level to promote venous return and decrease dependent edema. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T11#GNS213_U1_T11_h8)

question: Which of the following symptoms should a nurse instruct a patient with peripheral artery disease to report immediately?

options.A: Mild muscle cramping during a scheduled morning walk
options.B: Gradual skin discoloration around the ankles over several months
options.C: Sudden coldness, severe pain, and pallor in the extremity
options.D: A minor, slow-healing superficial scratch on the shin

explanation: Sudden coldness, severe pain, and pallor are classic indicators of acute limb ischemia, requiring immediate reporting and emergency intervention. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T11#GNS213_U1_T11_h8)

question: What is the primary focus of cardiovascular pathophysiology?

options.A: The study of normal embryonic heart development
options.B: Functional and structural changes in the heart and vessels during disease states
options.C: Surgical techniques for coronary bypass
options.D: Pharmacokinetics of over-the-counter analgesics

explanation: Cardiovascular pathophysiology specifically examines the functional and structural alterations that happen within the heart and blood vessels during various disease processes. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T12#GNS213_U1_T12_h1)

question: Why is understanding cardiovascular pathophysiology essential for nursing students in Nigeria?

options.A: It helps nurses anticipate complications and implement evidence-based interventions for rising cardiovascular diseases.
options.B: It replaces the need for clinical pharmacology in the hospital setting.
options.C: It is only required for passing board exams without clinical application.
options.D: It prevents the occurrence of infectious diseases like malaria.

explanation: Understanding pathophysiology allows nurses to anticipate complications, interpret diagnostics, and deliver evidence-based care for prevalent conditions like hypertension and heart failure. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T12#GNS213_U1_T12_h1)

question: Which hemodynamic parameter represents the volume of blood stretching the ventricles at the end of diastole?

options.A: Afterload
options.B: Contractility
options.C: Preload
options.D: Cardiac output

explanation: Preload is defined as the end-diastolic volume that stretches the ventricles prior to contraction, largely determined by venous return. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T12#GNS213_U1_T12_h2)

question: How is cardiac output calculated?

options.A: Stroke volume multiplied by heart rate
options.B: Blood pressure divided by systemic vascular resistance
options.C: Preload divided by afterload
options.D: Ejection fraction multiplied by systolic pressure

explanation: Cardiac output is the volume of blood pumped per minute and is calculated by multiplying the stroke volume by the heart rate. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T12#GNS213_U1_T12_h2)

question: What is the initial triggering event in the development of atherosclerosis?

options.A: Rupture of a stable fibrous cap
options.B: Endothelial injury caused by factors like hypertension or hyperlipidemia
options.C: Immediate conversion of smooth muscle cells into foam cells
options.D: Massive hemorrhage into the myocardial wall

explanation: Atherosclerosis begins with endothelial injury, which increases vessel permeability and permits lipid deposition in the subendothelial space. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T12#GNS213_U1_T12_h3)

question: Which cellular component primarily forms the fatty streak after engulfing oxidized LDL particles?

options.A: Erythrocytes
options.B: Platelets
options.C: Foam cells
options.D: Fibroblasts

explanation: Macrophages ingest oxidized LDL particles and transform into lipid-laden foam cells, which aggregate to create the early fatty streak. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T12#GNS213_U1_T12_h3)

question: Which neurohormonal system is chronically activated in heart failure, leading to sodium and water retention and maladaptive remodeling?

options.A: Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS)
options.B: Parasympathetic nervous system
options.C: Insulin-glucagon regulatory pathway
options.D: Thyroid hormone feedback loop

explanation: Chronic activation of the RAAS promotes systemic vasoconstriction and renal sodium and water retention, contributing to cardiac remodeling and fluid overload. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T12#GNS213_U1_T12_h4)

question: What is a primary clinical manifestation of left-sided heart failure?

options.A: Peripheral pitting pedal edema
options.B: Pulmonary congestion and dyspnea
options.C: Hepatomegaly and ascites
options.D: Jugular venous distension

explanation: Left-sided heart failure causes blood to back up into the pulmonary circulation, resulting in pulmonary congestion, shortness of breath, and orthopnea. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T12#GNS213_U1_T12_h4)

question: What is a primary functional driver of increased total peripheral resistance in hypertension?

options.A: Decreased cardiac output and bradycardia
options.B: Vascular remodeling and endothelial dysfunction
options.C: Massive vasodilation of peripheral arterioles
options.D: Increased synthesis of nitric oxide

explanation: Hypertension is driven by vascular remodeling and endothelial dysfunction, which reduce vessel lumen diameter and increase resistance. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T12#GNS213_U1_T12_h5)

question: How does endothelial dysfunction contribute to the pathophysiology of hypertension?

options.A: By increasing nitric oxide production and causing vasodilation
options.B: By decreasing vasodilators like nitric oxide and increasing vasoconstrictors like endothelin-1
options.C: By preventing any smooth muscle cell proliferation
options.D: By lowering renal sodium reabsorption rates

explanation: Endothelial dysfunction impairs vasodilator release while elevating vasoconstrictor substances, favoring persistent vascular constriction and elevated pressure. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T12#GNS213_U1_T12_h5)

question: What is the most common mechanism responsible for sustained tachyarrhythmias?

options.A: Enhanced vagal nerve stimulation
options.B: Re-entry circuits involving delayed conduction and unidirectional block
options.C: Complete third-degree atrioventricular block
options.D: Suppression of all automatic pacemaker cells

explanation: Re-entry circuits occur when an electrical impulse continuously loops through damaged tissue due to conduction delays, triggering rapid rhythms like tachycardias. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T12#GNS213_U1_T12_h6)

question: Where does the normal cardiac electrical impulse originate?

options.A: Atrioventricular (AV) node
options.B: Bundle of His
options.C: Sinoatrial (SA) node
options.D: Purkinje fiber network

explanation: The sinoatrial (SA) node acts as the primary natural pacemaker of the heart, initiating normal electrical impulses. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T12#GNS213_U1_T12_h6)

question: How is valvular stenosis defined pathophysiologically?

options.A: Failure of the valve leaflets to close completely, causing backward blood flow
options.B: Narrowing of the valve opening that impedes forward blood flow and creates a pressure gradient
options.C: Microbial vegetations destroying the chordae tendineae
options.D: Congenital absence of all heart chambers

explanation: Stenosis is the narrowing of a valve orifice, restricting forward blood flow and increasing the pressure work required by the heart chamber. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T12#GNS213_U1_T12_h7)

question: What is a frequent cause of fibrotic leaflet thickening and fusion resulting from an autoimmune reaction to streptococcal infection?

options.A: Rheumatic fever
options.B: Atherosclerosis
options.C: Essential hypertension
options.D: Myxomatous degeneration

explanation: Rheumatic fever is an inflammatory autoimmune condition following streptococcal infections that leads to chronic scarring, thickening, and fusion of heart valves. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T12#GNS213_U1_T12_h7)

question: Which nursing action is essential when caring for a patient on cardiovascular medications like ACE inhibitors and diuretics?

options.A: Monitoring for adverse drug effects and evaluating therapeutic hemodynamic responses
options.B: Encouraging a high-sodium diet to prevent hypotension
options.C: Discontinuing medication immediately upon symptom improvement
options.D: Avoiding any physical assessments of vital signs

explanation: Nurses must continuously monitor patients for adverse drug reactions and evaluate how well the medications manage hemodynamic status and symptoms. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T12#GNS213_U1_T12_h8)

question: What primary lifestyle modification should nurses educate cardiovascular patients about to help manage their condition?

options.A: High-fat, high-calorie meal planning
options.B: Low-sodium diet, smoking cessation, and weight management
options.C: Complete elimination of all physical movement and strict bedrest
options.D: Increasing daily caffeine intake

explanation: Patient education focuses on heart-healthy modifications such as adopting low-sodium diets, stopping smoking, and maintaining appropriate weight to reduce cardiac workload. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T12#GNS213_U1_T12_h8)

question: What is a primary responsibility of the nurse in cardiovascular care?

options.A: Diagnosing underlying cardiac structural anomalies
options.B: Recognizing subtle changes in hemodynamic status early
options.C: Prescribing initial antihypertensive drug therapy
options.D: Performing surgical revascularization procedures

explanation: Nurses are at the frontline of observing and recognizing subtle changes in a patient's hemodynamic status to ensure early intervention. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T13#GNS213_U1_T13_h1)

question: Why are cultural considerations and local realities important in Nigerian cardiovascular nursing practice?

options.A: They replace the need for pharmacological interventions
options.B: They allow nurses to tailor health messages to local diets and beliefs
options.C: They eliminate the necessity for interdisciplinary collaboration
options.D: They reduce the cost of operating hospital facilities

explanation: Tailoring health messages to local diets, beliefs, and economic realities ensures effective communication and patient compliance. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T13#GNS213_U1_T13_h1)

question: Which heart sound is frequently associated with heart failure during auscultation?

options.A: S1
options.B: S2
options.C: S3
options.D: A normal physiological click

explanation: An S3 heart sound is an extra sound that often indicates the presence of heart failure. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T13#GNS213_U1_T13_h2)

question: What is the primary purpose of continuous hemodynamic monitoring in cardiac patients?

options.A: To replace the need for physical examinations entirely
options.B: To provide real-time data on cardiac output and fluid status
options.C: To diagnose the exact genetic cause of a heart defect
options.D: To administer oral medications automatically

explanation: Continuous hemodynamic monitoring supplies real-time data regarding the patient's cardiac output and fluid status. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T13#GNS213_U1_T13_h2)

question: Which laboratory biomarker is specifically critical for diagnosing myocardial injury?

options.A: Serum creatinine
options.B: Troponin T or I
options.C: White blood cell count
options.D: Serum potassium

explanation: Cardiac biomarkers such as Troponin T and I are essential for diagnosing myocardial injury. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T13#GNS213_U1_T13_h3)

question: What is a key post-procedural nursing responsibility after a cardiac catheterization?

options.A: Encouraging immediate heavy physical exercise
options.B: Monitoring the vascular insertion site for bleeding or hematoma
options.C: Removing vascular closure devices independently without training
options.D: Withholding all fluids indefinitely

explanation: Post-procedural care requires frequent monitoring of the insertion site for bleeding or hematoma formation, along with checking distal pulses. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T13#GNS213_U1_T13_h3)

question: What vital parameter must a nurse check before administering digoxin to a patient?

options.A: Respiratory rate
options.B: Apical pulse rate
options.C: Body temperature
options.D: Abdominal girth

explanation: Nurses must measure the apical pulse before giving digoxin and hold the medication if the rate is below safe thresholds, typically 60 beats per minute. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T13#GNS213_U1_T13_h4)

question: What is the primary clinical purpose of administering antiplatelet and anticoagulant medications?

options.A: To decrease heart valve calcification
options.B: To prevent thrombus formation
options.C: To lower serum cholesterol levels
options.D: To increase resting heart rate

explanation: Antiplatelets and anticoagulants are prescribed to prevent blood clots or thrombus formation in conditions like coronary artery disease. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T13#GNS213_U1_T13_h4)

question: What is the appropriate initial patient positioning for someone experiencing acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary edema?

options.A: Flat supine position
options.B: Trendelenburg position
options.C: High-Fowler's position
options.D: Prone position

explanation: Placing the patient in an upright, high-Fowler's position helps decrease venous return to the heart and eases respiratory distress. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T13#GNS213_U1_T13_h5)

question: What immediate action should a nurse take when a patient presents with symptoms of an acute myocardial infarction?

options.A: Discharge the patient home for rest
options.B: Initiate the emergency protocol, obtain a stat ECG, and administer oxygen
options.C: Wait for laboratory troponin results before any intervention
options.D: Encourage the patient to perform heavy physical activity

explanation: Rapid response for an acute myocardial infarction includes getting a stat ECG, applying oxygen, and initiating urgent medical management. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T13#GNS213_U1_T13_h5)

question: Which dietary modification is typically recommended for patients with cardiovascular disorders like hypertension and heart failure?

options.A: A high-sodium and high-fat diet
options.B: A low-sodium and low-cholesterol diet
options.C: A strictly carbohydrate-free diet
options.D: An entirely liquid-only diet

explanation: Adopting a low-sodium and low-cholesterol diet is crucial for managing blood pressure and reducing cardiac workload. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T13#GNS213_U1_T13_h6)

question: What warning sign should patients be taught to report immediately to healthcare providers?

options.A: Gradual improvement in exercise tolerance
options.B: Sudden chest pain or worsening shortness of breath
options.C: Stable daily weight measurements
options.D: Mild fatigue after a full night of sleep

explanation: Sudden chest pain or worsening shortness of breath are red-flag symptoms that require immediate medical evaluation. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T13#GNS213_U1_T13_h6)

question: What is a primary goal of a structured cardiac rehabilitation program?

options.A: To completely cure congenital heart anomalies
options.B: To restore optimal physical, psychological, and social functioning
options.C: To eliminate the need for any future medical check-ups
options.D: To replace pharmacological therapy with physical training

explanation: Cardiac rehabilitation focuses on restoring optimal physical, psychological, and social well-being for patients recovering from heart events. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T13#GNS213_U1_T13_h7)

question: How do nursing interventions in long-term cardiac care impact patient outcomes?

options.A: They increase hospital readmission rates
options.B: They reduce mortality and enhance quality of life
options.C: They prevent patients from engaging in any physical activity
options.D: They isolate patients from community health resources

explanation: Fostering self-care and long-term support significantly reduces mortality and enhances the overall quality of life for cardiac patients. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T13#GNS213_U1_T13_h7)

question: Which of the following is a primary driver of maladaptive changes during chronic cardiac impairment?

options.A: Activation of compensatory mechanisms
options.B: Immediate normalization of blood pressure
options.C: Permanent cessation of sympathetic output
options.D: Instantaneous myocardial regeneration

explanation: Compensatory mechanisms like the sympathetic nervous system are initially helpful but become maladaptive over time, leading to worsening cardiac status. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T14#GNS213_U1_T14_h1)

question: Why is understanding cardiovascular complications particularly important for nursing practice in Nigeria?

options.A: Cardiovascular diseases are completely eradicated
options.B: Cardiovascular conditions are increasingly prevalent
options.C: Complications only occur in surgical patients
options.D: Nurses are solely responsible for prescribing cardiac medications

explanation: Cardiovascular diseases are increasingly prevalent across local healthcare settings in Nigeria, making complication awareness crucial. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T14#GNS213_U1_T14_h1)

question: Which clinical manifestation is most characteristic of left-sided heart failure?

options.A: Hepatomegaly
options.B: Jugular venous distention
options.C: Pulmonary congestion and orthopnea
options.D: Dependent pitting ankle edema

explanation: Left-sided heart failure causes fluid to back up into the pulmonary circulation, leading to respiratory symptoms like pulmonary congestion and orthopnea. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T14#GNS213_U1_T14_h2)

question: What is a primary nursing responsibility when monitoring a patient with hemodynamic instability from heart failure?

options.A: Encouraging high sodium intake
options.B: Tracking daily weights and fluid balance
options.C: Discontinuing all diuretic therapy immediately
options.D: Restricting patient physical therapy forever

explanation: Tracking daily weights and monitoring intake and output are crucial nursing responsibilities to evaluate fluid balance and detect worsening heart failure. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T14#GNS213_U1_T14_h2)

question: Which rhythm disturbance is considered an immediate life-threatening emergency requiring rapid defibrillation?

options.A: Sinus bradycardia
options.B: Ventricular fibrillation
options.C: First-degree heart block
options.D: Controlled atrial fibrillation

explanation: Ventricular fibrillation results in an immediate loss of effective cardiac output and requires rapid defibrillation to save the patient's life. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T14#GNS213_U1_T14_h3)

question: Why is chronic atrial fibrillation a significant risk factor for stroke?

options.A: It causes immediate closure of the carotid arteries
options.B: It leads to blood stasis within the atria
options.C: It dramatically lowers systemic blood pressure
options.D: It permanently stops all electrical activity

explanation: Atrial fibrillation causes irregular and ineffective atrial contractions, leading to blood stasis that can form clots and travel to the brain. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T14#GNS213_U1_T14_h3)

question: Which of the following describes components of Virchow's triad predisposing a patient to thrombosis?

options.A: Endothelial injury, hypercoagulability, and venous stasis
options.B: Hypokalemia, hypertension, and tachycardia
options.C: Dehydration, hyperthermia, and polycythemia
options.D: Bradycardia, hypotension, and vasodilation

explanation: Virchow's triad consists of endothelial injury, hypercoagulability, and venous stasis, which together promote thrombus formation. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T14#GNS213_U1_T14_h4)

question: What is a classic symptom of a pulmonary embolism resulting from a dislodged thrombus?

options.A: Localized lower leg redness only
options.B: Sudden dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain
options.C: Severe hypertension and bradycardia
options.D: Unilateral facial drooping and slurred speech

explanation: Obstruction of pulmonary blood flow causes acute respiratory symptoms such as sudden dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T14#GNS213_U1_T14_h4)

question: What is the primary underlying pathophysiology of cardiogenic shock?

options.A: Massive vasodilation from a bacterial infection
options.B: Acute severe impairment of myocardial pumping function
options.C: Severe hypovolemia due to acute hemorrhage
options.D: Mechanical obstruction of the superior vena cava

explanation: Cardiogenic shock is caused by severe pump failure, leading to inadequate tissue perfusion despite adequate intravascular volume. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T14#GNS213_U1_T14_h5)

question: Which clinical sign is indicative of poor end-organ perfusion in a patient with cardiogenic shock?

options.A: Warm, flushed extremities
options.B: Bounding peripheral pulses
options.C: Oliguria and altered mental status
options.D: Polyuria and hypertension

explanation: Oliguria (low urine output) and altered mental status reflect inadequate blood flow to the kidneys and brain during shock. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T14#GNS213_U1_T14_h5)

question: What is a primary consequence of ventricular free wall rupture following a myocardial infarction?

options.A: Acute cardiac tamponade and rapid collapse
options.B: Chronic stable angina over several years
options.C: Isolated hypertension with bradycardia
options.D: Permanent normalization of heart rhythm

explanation: Rupture of the ventricular free wall causes blood to leak into the pericardial space, resulting in cardiac tamponade and rapid circulatory collapse. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T14#GNS213_U1_T14_h6)

question: What physical finding is commonly associated with an acute interventricular septal rupture?

options.A: A new, loud systolic murmur
options.B: An absent radial pulse
options.C: Tracheal deviation
options.D: Clear, uncompromised lung sounds

explanation: An acute ventricular septal defect creates abnormal shunting of blood, which manifests as a new, loud systolic murmur. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T14#GNS213_U1_T14_h6)

question: Which nursing assessment finding suggests worsening fluid overload in a cardiovascular patient?

options.A: Clear, bilateral breath sounds
options.B: Presence of crackles in the lung bases
options.C: Absence of peripheral edema
options.D: Normal jugular venous pressure

explanation: Crackles in the lung bases indicate fluid accumulation in the alveoli, a hallmark of fluid overload and worsening heart failure. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T14#GNS213_U1_T14_h7)

question: What is the clinical value of monitoring brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) levels?

options.A: It diagnoses bacterial endocarditis
options.B: It evaluates myocardial injury and heart failure status
options.C: It measures blood clotting time
options.D: It identifies acute electrolyte deficiencies

explanation: BNP is a biomarker released by stretched ventricular tissue, providing objective data on heart failure severity and fluid status. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T14#GNS213_U1_T14_h7)

question: What is a primary nursing responsibility during emergency cardiovascular interventions?

options.A: Discontinuing all monitoring equipment
options.B: Preparing emergency equipment and administering medications safely
options.C: Discharging the patient immediately without instructions
options.D: Performing invasive surgery independently

explanation: Nurses must prepare emergency equipment, administer medications correctly, and continuously monitor the patient during acute interventions. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T14#GNS213_U1_T14_h8)

question: Which class of medication is commonly used to reduce myocardial workload and heart rate in cardiac emergencies?

options.A: Beta-blockers
options.B: Vasoconstrictors
options.C: Prophylactic antibiotics
options.D: Osmotic laxatives

explanation: Beta-blockers slow the heart rate and decrease myocardial contractility, thereby reducing the heart's oxygen demand during acute conditions. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T14#GNS213_U1_T14_h8)

question: Which level of prevention aims to prevent the development of risk factors in an entire population, often starting in childhood?

options.A: Primordial prevention
options.B: Secondary prevention
options.C: Tertiary prevention
options.D: Diagnostic prevention

explanation: Primordial prevention focuses on preventing the actual development of risk factors within a population, typically beginning early in life through healthy lifestyle education. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T15#GNS213_U1_T15_h1)

question: What is the primary focus of secondary prevention in cardiovascular disease management?

options.A: Preventing the initial formation of risk factors
options.B: Rehabilitation for advanced heart failure
options.C: Early diagnosis and prompt treatment to prevent recurrent events
options.D: Community-wide policy making on tobacco use

explanation: Secondary prevention is centered on early detection and timely treatment of existing conditions to halt disease progression and prevent recurrent cardiovascular events. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T15#GNS213_U1_T15_h1)

question: Which of the following represents a non-modifiable cardiovascular risk factor?

options.A: Hypertension
options.B: Cigarette smoking
options.C: Advanced age
options.D: Physical inactivity

explanation: Advanced age is a non-modifiable risk factor because an individual's age cannot be changed through lifestyle or medical interventions. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T15#GNS213_U1_T15_h2)

question: Why is it important for nurses to identify both modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors?

options.A: To eliminate all genetic risks completely
options.B: To target changeable behaviors and closely monitor high-risk individuals
options.C: To diagnose psychiatric disorders in cardiac patients
options.D: To determine the patient's exact date of discharge

explanation: Recognizing non-modifiable risks highlights who needs closer monitoring, while identifying modifiable risks allows nurses to guide patients in making healthy lifestyle changes. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T15#GNS213_U1_T15_h2)

question: Which dietary component is directly linked to an increased risk of hypertension and should be limited?

options.A: Omega-3 fatty acids
options.B: Sodium
options.C: Dietary fiber
options.D: Whole grains

explanation: Excessive sodium intake is directly linked to elevated blood pressure, making salt restriction essential in preventing and managing hypertension. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T15#GNS213_U1_T15_h3)

question: How does adequate dietary fiber assist in cardiovascular health?

options.A: It increases blood pressure rapidly
options.B: It adds trans fats to the bloodstream
options.C: It helps manage cholesterol levels
options.D: It replaces the need for physical activity

explanation: Dietary fiber helps manage cholesterol levels by binding to bile acids in the digestive tract, promoting their excretion from the body. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T15#GNS213_U1_T15_h3)

question: What is the recommended minimum duration of moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity per week for cardiovascular health?

options.A: 30 minutes
options.B: 75 minutes
options.C: 150 minutes
options.D: 300 minutes

explanation: Current guidelines recommend at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity per week to maintain and improve cardiovascular health. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T15#GNS213_U1_T15_h4)

question: Which of the following is a direct cardiovascular benefit of regular exercise?

options.A: Increasing resting heart rate to maximum levels
options.B: Raising high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol
options.C: Decreasing insulin sensitivity
options.D: Promoting LDL cholesterol accumulation

explanation: Regular physical activity optimizes lipid profiles by increasing HDL (good) cholesterol and lowering triglycerides and LDL cholesterol. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T15#GNS213_U1_T15_h4)

question: What effect does cigarette smoke have on the cardiovascular system that promotes thrombus formation?

options.A: It decreases platelet aggregation
options.B: It causes endothelial injury and increases platelet aggregation
options.C: It lowers resting heart rate and blood pressure
options.D: It enhances endothelial repair mechanisms

explanation: Constituents of cigarette smoke cause direct injury to the vascular endothelium and increase platelet aggregation, facilitating blood clot formation. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T15#GNS213_U1_T15_h5)

question: Which framework is commonly utilized by nurses to assess and intervene regarding a patient's smoking status?

options.A: The ABCDE triage system
options.B: The 5 As framework
options.C: The SOAP note method
options.D: The GCS scoring tool

explanation: The '5 As' framework (Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange) is a structured, evidence-based approach used by healthcare providers to guide smoking cessation counseling. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T15#GNS213_U1_T15_h5)

question: Why is hypertension frequently referred to as the 'silent killer'?

options.A: It causes immediate, painful cardiac arrest
options.B: It presents with no outward symptoms in its early stages
options.C: It only occurs during sleep
options.D: It is completely untreatable with medication

explanation: Hypertension is called the silent killer because it typically develops without causing any noticeable symptoms, making routine screening critical for early detection. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T15#GNS213_U1_T15_h6)

question: Which of the following parameters is evaluated as part of a standard lipid profile screening?

options.A: Blood glucose levels
options.B: Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol
options.C: Hemoglobin concentration
options.D: Platelet count

explanation: A standard lipid profile measures components such as total cholesterol, HDL, triglycerides, and LDL cholesterol to assess cardiovascular risk. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T15#GNS213_U1_T15_h6)

question: How does chronic psychological stress negatively impact the cardiovascular system?

options.A: By suppressing the sympathetic nervous system entirely
options.B: By causing sustained activation of neurohormonal pathways that elevate blood pressure and inflammation
options.C: By permanently lowering cortisol and catecholamine levels
options.D: By directly increasing HDL cholesterol production

explanation: Chronic stress activates the sympathetic nervous system and hormone pathways, leading to high blood pressure, increased heart rate, and systemic inflammation. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T15#GNS213_U1_T15_h7)

question: Why is it important for nurses to identify clinical depression in cardiac patients?

options.A: Depression guarantees absolute adherence to medication
options.B: Depression is an independent risk factor for poor cardiovascular outcomes
options.C: Depression automatically normalizes blood pressure
options.D: Depression eliminates the need for dietary modifications

explanation: Clinical depression is recognized as an independent risk factor for adverse cardiovascular events and can negatively impact a patient's adherence to treatment. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T15#GNS213_U1_T15_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of using the teach-back method during patient education?

options.A: To test the nurse's teaching ability
options.B: To verify that the patient has accurately understood the health information
options.C: To replace the need for written discharge instructions
options.D: To diagnose underlying psychiatric disorders

explanation: The teach-back method allows nurses to confirm patient comprehension by asking patients to explain the instructions back in their own words. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T15#GNS213_U1_T15_h8)

question: How do community outreach programs contribute to cardiovascular disease prevention?

options.A: By providing advanced open-heart surgeries in remote villages
options.B: By offering screenings, public awareness seminars, and addressing health disparities
options.C: By eliminating all genetic risk factors within a region
options.D: By replacing hospital-based emergency care entirely

explanation: Community outreach programs improve public health by offering accessible screenings, raising awareness, and addressing healthcare access gaps in underserved populations. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T15#GNS213_U1_T15_h8)

question: What is the primary function of an electrocardiogram (ECG)?

options.A: To measure blood pressure within the chambers
options.B: To record the electrical activity of the heart
options.C: To visualize the physical heart valves using ultrasound
options.D: To measure the oxygen saturation of arterial blood

explanation: An ECG is a non-invasive test specifically designed to record and display the electrical activity of the heart over time. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T16#GNS213_U1_T16_h1)

question: How does the ECG machine detect the heart's electrical impulses?

options.A: Through specialized electrodes placed on the patient's skin
options.B: Through an invasive catheter inserted into the femoral artery
options.C: By measuring temperature changes across the chest wall
options.D: By listening to heart sounds with an electronic stethoscope

explanation: The machine detects tiny electrical impulses through electrodes attached to the surface of the patient's skin. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T16#GNS213_U1_T16_h1)

question: Which structure acts as the natural pacemaker of the heart?

options.A: Atrioventricular (AV) node
options.B: Bundle of His
options.C: Sinoatrial (SA) node
options.D: Purkinje fibers

explanation: The sinoatrial (SA) node is recognized as the heart's natural pacemaker, initiating the electrical impulses that drive the cardiac cycle. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T16#GNS213_U1_T16_h2)

question: What primary cellular event occurs during cardiac cell depolarization?

options.A: Rapid influx of sodium ions into the cell
options.B: Massive outflow of calcium ions
options.C: Accumulation of negative potassium inside
options.D: Immediate cell death and necrosis

explanation: Depolarization is characterized by a rapid influx of sodium ions into the cell, which changes the interior charge from negative to positive. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T16#GNS213_U1_T16_h2)

question: How many total physical electrodes are placed on the patient to record a standard 12-lead ECG?

options.A: 6 electrodes
options.B: 10 electrodes
options.C: 12 electrodes
options.D: 14 electrodes

explanation: A standard 12-lead ECG uses 10 physical electrodes to generate 12 different electrical views (leads) of the heart. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T16#GNS213_U1_T16_h3)

question: Where is the V1 electrode precisely placed on the patient's chest?

options.A: Fourth intercostal space at the right sternal border
options.B: Fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line
options.C: Fourth intercostal space at the left sternal border
options.D: Fifth intercostal space at the midaxillary line

explanation: V1 is placed in the fourth intercostal space at the right sternal border, serving as an anatomical landmark for chest lead placement. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T16#GNS213_U1_T16_h3)

question: What cardiac event does the P wave represent on a normal ECG?

options.A: Ventricular repolarization
options.B: Atrial depolarization
options.C: Atrial repolarization
options.D: Ventricular depolarization

explanation: The P wave represents atrial depolarization, which is the electrical activation of the left and right atria. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T16#GNS213_U1_T16_h4)

question: An abnormal elevation or depression of which ECG component is a key indicator of myocardial ischemia?

options.A: P wave
options.B: PR interval
options.C: ST segment
options.D: QT interval

explanation: The ST segment represents early ventricular repolarization, and its deviation from the baseline is a primary sign of ischemia or infarction. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T16#GNS213_U1_T16_h4)

question: What is the normal duration range for a healthy PR interval?

options.A: 0.02 to 0.05 seconds
options.B: 0.12 to 0.20 seconds
options.C: 0.25 to 0.35 seconds
options.D: 0.40 to 0.50 seconds

explanation: A normal PR interval lasts between 0.12 and 0.20 seconds, representing normal conduction time from atria to ventricles. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T16#GNS213_U1_T16_h5)

question: How can a nurse quickly calculate the heart rate from a 6-second ECG strip?

options.A: Count the total number of small boxes and divide by 1500
options.B: Count the number of R waves and multiply by 10
options.C: Measure the distance between two T waves in millimeters
options.D: Count the P waves and multiply by 6

explanation: On a standard 6-second ECG strip, counting the number of R waves and multiplying by 10 provides a quick estimation of the ventricular heart rate per minute. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T16#GNS213_U1_T16_h5)

question: Which ECG characteristic is a hallmark of atrial fibrillation?

options.A: Regularly regular rhythm with very tall T waves
options.B: Irregularly irregular rhythm with absent P waves
options.C: A fixed heart rate of exactly 150 beats per minute
options.D: Prolonged PR intervals exceeding 0.30 seconds

explanation: Atrial fibrillation is clinically identified by an irregularly irregular rhythm and the absence of discrete P waves on the ECG. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T16#GNS213_U1_T16_h6)

question: Which of the following rhythms is considered an immediate life-threatening emergency requiring resuscitation?

options.A: Sinus bradycardia
options.B: Sinus tachycardia
options.C: Ventricular fibrillation
options.D: First-degree AV block

explanation: Ventricular fibrillation (VF) produces no effective cardiac output and requires immediate cardiopulmonary resuscitation and defibrillation. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T16#GNS213_U1_T16_h6)

question: What classic ECG finding indicates acute myocardial injury?

options.A: Prolonged PR interval
options.B: ST segment elevation
options.C: Flattened P waves
options.D: Narrowed QRS complex

explanation: ST segment elevation is the classic electrocardiographic sign indicating acute myocardial injury and potential transmural infarction. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T16#GNS213_U1_T16_h7)

question: Which ECG leads correspond to an inferior wall myocardial infarction?

options.B: I, aVL, V5, V6
options.C: II, III, aVF
options.D: aVR, V1, V6

explanation: Leads II, III, and aVF view the inferior surface of the heart and show changes during an inferior wall myocardial infarction. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T16#GNS213_U1_T16_h7)

question: Why is proper skin preparation necessary prior to applying ECG electrodes?

options.A: To increase the patient's body temperature
options.B: To remove oils and hair that can cause artifact interference
options.C: To stimulate the sinoatrial node for a stronger signal
options.D: To prevent local skin allergic reactions to the gel

explanation: Cleaning the skin and removing oils or hair ensures optimal electrical contact between the electrode and skin, minimizing artifact interference. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T16#GNS213_U1_T16_h8)

question: What instruction should the nurse give to the patient during the ECG recording?

options.A: Hold your breath completely for 60 seconds
options.B: Remain still and breathe normally without talking
options.C: Sit upright and flex your arms tightly
options.D: Walk slowly around the bed while leads are attached

explanation: Patients should remain still, relaxed, and breathe normally without talking to prevent muscle movement artifacts from distorting the ECG tracing. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T16#GNS213_U1_T16_h8)

question: What are the primary clinical indications for emergency defibrillation?

options.A: Asystole and Pulseless Electrical Activity
options.B: Ventricular Fibrillation and Pulseless Ventricular Tachycardia
options.C: Symptomatic Bradycardia and Third-Degree Heart Block
options.D: Atrial Fibrillation with Rapid Ventricular Response

explanation: Defibrillation is specifically indicated for shockable cardiac arrest rhythms, which include Ventricular Fibrillation and Pulseless Ventricular Tachycardia. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T17#GNS213_U1_T17_h1)

question: What is the primary physiological mechanism of action during defibrillation?

options.A: Depolarizing a critical mass of heart muscle cells to reset the cardiac rhythm
options.B: Accelerating the heart rate by supplying continuous electrical energy to the sinoatrial node
options.C: Cooling the myocardial tissue to reduce oxygen consumption during arrest
options.D: Contracting the ventricles mechanically through external chest wall pressure

explanation: Defibrillation delivers a therapeutic electrical current that depolarizes a critical mass of myocardium simultaneously, allowing the heart's natural pacemaker to take over. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T17#GNS213_U1_T17_h1)

question: How does Ventricular Fibrillation (VF) typically present on an electrocardiogram (ECG)?

options.A: Regular, slow QRS complexes with normal PR intervals
options.B: Irregular, chaotic baseline oscillations without discernible QRS complexes
options.C: Wide QRS complexes preceded by upright P waves at a normal rate
options.D: Prolonged PR intervals followed by dropped ventricular beats

explanation: VF appears on an ECG as chaotic, irregular baseline oscillations lacking any recognizable P waves, QRS complexes, or T waves. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T17#GNS213_U1_T17_h2)

question: Why does Pulseless Ventricular Tachycardia (pVT) result in a lack of cardiac output?

options.A: The heart rate is too slow to generate adequate stroke volume.
options.B: Atrioventricular dissociation prevents any electrical activity from reaching the ventricles.
options.C: The excessively rapid heart rate severely compromises ventricular filling time.
options.D: The atria contract simultaneously with the ventricles, destroying valve function.

explanation: In pVT, the heart rate is extremely fast, which drastically reduces the time available for the ventricles to fill with blood, eliminating cardiac output. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T17#GNS213_U1_T17_h2)

question: What is a key operational difference of a monophasic defibrillator compared to a biphasic defibrillator?

options.A: It delivers electrical current in a single, unidirectional path.
options.B: It requires significantly lower energy settings to terminate VF.
options.C: It automatically adjusts energy based on patient impedance.
options.D: It alternates polarity during every chest compression cycle.

explanation: Monophasic defibrillators deliver current in only one direction, necessitating higher energy levels to achieve successful cardioversion or defibrillation. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T17#GNS213_U1_T17_h3)

question: What is a major clinical advantage of using a biphasic defibrillator?

options.A: It eliminates the need for conductive gel or pads.
options.B: It achieves high success rates at lower energy levels, reducing myocardial injury.
options.C: It can convert non-shockable rhythms into perfusing rhythms automatically.
options.D: It operates exclusively on internal pacemaker battery sources.

explanation: Biphasic waveforms are more efficient, allowing successful termination of arrhythmias at lower energy levels and causing less post-shock myocardial damage. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T17#GNS213_U1_T17_h3)

question: Why must oxygen delivery devices be moved away from the patient's chest during defibrillation?

options.A: To prevent accidental disconnection of the oxygen tubing
options.B: To prevent the risk of sparking and fire in an oxygen-rich environment
options.C: To ensure the defibrillator pads make full contact with the skin
options.D: To allow the nurse room to place manual paddles correctly

explanation: Oxygen supports combustion, and an electrical spark from a defibrillator near free-flowing oxygen can cause a serious fire. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T17#GNS213_U1_T17_h4)

question: What is the recommended nursing action regarding defibrillator pad placement in a patient with an implanted pacemaker?

options.A: Place the pad directly over the pacemaker generator to ensure energy transfer.
options.B: Place the pads at least one inch away from the pacemaker generator.
options.C: Turn off the pacemaker externally before placing any pads on the chest.
options.D: Avoid using the defibrillator entirely if a pacemaker is present.

explanation: Pads should be placed at least one inch away from implanted devices to protect the hardware from damage and ensure effective energy delivery. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T17#GNS213_U1_T17_h4)

question: What action should the healthcare team take immediately after delivering a defibrillation shock?

options.A: Check the patient's pulse and blood pressure for recovery signs.
options.B: Immediately resume high-quality CPR for two minutes.
options.C: Administer a routine dose of intravenous calcium chloride.
options.D: Turn off the monitor to conserve battery power.

explanation: After a shock, CPR must be resumed immediately for two minutes before checking the rhythm again, accounting for myocardial stunning. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T17#GNS213_U1_T17_h5)

question: Where is the standard anterolateral pad placement located for adult defibrillation?

options.A: Right upper sternal border and left mid-axillary line apex
options.B: Left upper sternal border and right mid-clavicular line apex
options.C: Directly over the center of the manubrium and epigastric region
options.D: Both pads placed vertically along the left paravertebral border

explanation: Standard pad placement requires one pad at the right upper sternal border below the clavicle and the second pad at the apex in the left mid-axillary line. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T17#GNS213_U1_T17_h5)

question: What primary clinical finding indicates that a patient has achieved Return of Spontaneous Circulation (ROSC)?

options.A: The appearance of regular sinus complexes combined with palpable pulses and blood pressure.
options.B: The immediate normalization of arterial blood gas values.
options.C: The complete cessation of all spontaneous breathing efforts.
options.D: A drop in body temperature to hypothermic baseline levels.

explanation: ROSC is confirmed when the patient displays signs of life, including a palpable pulse, measurable blood pressure, and an organized perfusing rhythm. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T17#GNS213_U1_T17_h6)

question: Why is continuous ECG monitoring critical immediately following successful defibrillation?

options.A: To calibrate the automatic internal defibrillator settings
options.B: To detect early recurrence of ventricular arrhythmias or conduction disturbances
options.C: To ensure the patient does not develop electrolyte imbalances
options.D: To verify that the pacemaker capture threshold remains stable

explanation: Continuous monitoring helps nurses promptly identify the recurrence of lethal rhythms or new arrhythmias that frequently follow cardiac arrest. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T17#GNS213_U1_T17_h6)

question: What should a nurse suspect if the defibrillator monitor displays a high transthoracic impedance or poor pad contact error?

options.A: The patient has an internal pacemaker malfunction.
options.B: There is poor pad adhesion, excessive moisture, or air pockets under the electrodes.
options.C: The battery pack has completely depleted its charge.
options.D: The synchronization mode is actively engaged.

explanation: High impedance errors usually result from poor contact, moisture, or trapped air under the pads, which impedes electrical current flow. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T17#GNS213_U1_T17_h7)

question: What is a common cutaneous complication associated with repeated electrical shocks during defibrillation?

options.A: Subcutaneous emphysema
options.B: Thermal skin burns and erythema
options.C: Localized muscle hypertrophy
options.D: Contact dermatitis from silver-plated wires

explanation: The delivery of high electrical energy across the chest wall can cause thermal skin burns or blistering if pad contact is suboptimal. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T17#GNS213_U1_T17_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of conducting a systematic cardiovascular assessment?

options.A: To diagnose psychiatric disorders in cardiac patients
options.B: To detect actual or potential cardiovascular problems early
options.C: To replace the need for physician consultations
options.D: To determine the exact financial cost of hospital stay

explanation: A systematic cardiovascular assessment helps nurses detect actual or potential health problems early, facilitating prompt interventions and better patient outcomes. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T2#GNS213_U1_T2_h1)

question: Which of the following components is essential for a thorough cardiovascular evaluation?

options.A: Health history and physical examination only
options.B: Surgical intervention and physical therapy
options.C: Health history, physical examination, and diagnostic investigations
options.D: Nutritional counseling and discharge planning alone

explanation: A comprehensive cardiovascular evaluation integrates a health history, a focused physical examination, and the interpretation of relevant diagnostic investigations. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T2#GNS213_U1_T2_h1)

question: Which mnemonic is commonly used by nurses to thoroughly evaluate chest pain or discomfort during a health history?

options.A: ABCDE
options.B: PQRST
options.C: SOAP
options.D: PERRLA

explanation: The PQRST mnemonic stands for Provocation, Quality, Region/Radiation, Severity, and Time, which helps nurses systematically evaluate pain characteristics. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T2#GNS213_U1_T2_h2)

question: Why is it important to assess social history and lifestyle habits during a cardiovascular health history in Nigeria?

options.A: To determine the patient's exact religious beliefs
options.B: To evaluate risk factors like smoking, diet, and traditional medicine use that affect heart health
options.C: To check if the patient owns a vehicle
options.D: To calculate the hospital bill accurately

explanation: Assessing lifestyle habits, dietary patterns, and traditional medicine use helps identify key risk factors and barriers to cardiovascular health and treatment adherence. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T2#GNS213_U1_T2_h2)

question: What does jugular venous distension (JVD) primarily indicate during the physical assessment?

options.A: Elevated right atrial pressure
options.B: Normal left ventricular function
options.C: Dehydration and low blood volume
options.D: Peripheral arterial disease

explanation: Jugular venous distension reflects an elevation in right atrial pressure, commonly seen in right-sided heart failure or fluid overload. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T2#GNS213_U1_T2_h3)

question: Which part of the stethoscope is typically used for listening to high-pitched heart sounds such as S1 and S2?

options.A: The bell
options.B: The tubing
options.C: The diaphragm
options.D: The earpieces

explanation: The diaphragm of the stethoscope is best suited for transmitting high-pitched sounds like normal S1 and S2 heart sounds. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T2#GNS213_U1_T2_h3)

question: Which of the following cardiac biomarkers is considered highly specific for diagnosing myocardial injury or infarction?

options.A: Troponin
options.B: Hemoglobin
options.C: Serum creatinine
options.D: Albumin

explanation: Cardiac troponins (Troponin I and T) are gold standard biomarkers due to their high specificity and sensitivity for myocardial muscle injury. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T2#GNS213_U1_T2_h4)

question: What is the primary function of a 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG)?

options.A: To measure the amount of oxygen dissolved in the blood
options.B: To assess the electrical activity of the heart
options.C: To visualize the physical movement of heart valves
options.D: To determine the lipid and cholesterol levels

explanation: A 12-lead ECG records the electrical impulses generated by the heart, helping nurses and physicians identify arrhythmias and ischemic events. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T2#GNS213_U1_T2_h4)

question: What does the acronym SBAR stand for in clinical reporting?

options.A: System, Breathing, Assessment, Resuscitation
options.B: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation
options.C: Symptoms, Blood pressure, Action, Result
options.D: State, Bedside, Analysis, Reporting

explanation: SBAR stands for Situation, Background, Assessment, and Recommendation, which is a structured communication tool used to hand over critical patient information safely. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T2#GNS213_U1_T2_h5)

question: Why is immediate reporting of critical cardiovascular findings essential in Nigerian clinical practice?

options.A: To fulfill administrative paperwork requirements for hospital management
options.B: To prevent delayed medical interventions and ensure patient safety
options.C: To reduce the financial cost of medications
options.D: To determine visiting hours for family members

explanation: Prompt reporting of acute changes like severe chest pain or arrhythmias ensures that life-saving medical interventions can be initiated quickly to protect patient safety. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T2#GNS213_U1_T2_h5)

question: What is the primary definition of a cardiac dysrhythmia?

options.A: A permanent cessation of all heart sounds
options.B: Any abnormality in the rate, rhythm, origin, or conduction of cardiac electrical impulses
options.C: An infection of the inner heart muscle lining
options.D: A complete blockage of the coronary arteries

explanation: A cardiac dysrhythmia is defined as any disturbance or abnormality in the rate, rhythm, origin, or conduction of electrical impulses within the heart. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T3#GNS213_U1_T3_h1)

question: Why is understanding cardiac dysrhythmias essential for nursing students?

options.A: It helps them diagnose congenital heart diseases without equipment
options.B: It allows them to anticipate complications and initiate safe, evidence-based care
options.C: It replaces the need for physician consultations in emergency settings
options.D: It is only required for surgical theater nurses

explanation: Understanding dysrhythmias enables nurses to anticipate complications, initiate timely interventions, and provide safe care for patients experiencing rhythm disturbances. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T3#GNS213_U1_T3_h1)

question: Which structure is known as the natural pacemaker of the heart?

options.A: Atrioventricular node
options.B: Bundle of His
options.C: Sinoatrial node
options.D: Purkinje fibers

explanation: The sinoatrial (SA) node is recognized as the natural pacemaker of the heart because it initiates electrical impulses at an intrinsic rate of 60 to 100 beats per minute. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T3#GNS213_U1_T3_h2)
